About this work

Liber de Triplici Regione Claustralium et Spirituali Exercitio Monachorum — "On the Threefold Region of Cloister-dwellers and the Spiritual Exercise of Monks" — is Trithemius's ascetic guide for monks, charting interior progress through three "regions" or stages of discipline: purification, illumination, and union with God — a Pseudo-Dionysian scheme adapted to Benedictine observance. He finished it in manuscript in 1497; it was first printed at Mainz by Peter von Friedberg on 8 August 1498, and it is one of the central texts of his Sponheim reform programme.

This is the 1498 Mainz edition (e-rara witness) — printed by Peter von Friedberg, one of three witnesses of the De Triplici Regione in this corpus: this 1498 Mainz first printing, the 1498 BSB witness (prdl-24385), and the 1516 Leipzig reprint (prdl-24386). The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. No published English translation is known; the translation sits in the top tier (S).

Epistle of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to the little work On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Persons.

To the reverend fathers in Christ, the lord presidents, definitors, and the other abbots of the annual chapter of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the Bursfeld union and observance: brother Johannes, called Trithemius, abbot in Sponheim, of the same order and congregation, in the diocese of Mainz, sends reverence and charity.

I have obeyed your commands, most venerable fathers, and, as you instructed me, have undertaken to correct the little work On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Persons, together with the spiritual exercise of monks, lately edited by the venerable father lord Johannes, abbot of Bursfeld. And truly, had your authority not compelled me, I should never have dared to lay a hand on the distinguished work of so great a father, who, it is clear, being far more learned and holier than I, wrote excellently. For what could I correct, where everything is found most approved? A good and devout man, he wrote no otherwise than as he lives and [teaches?].

Nevertheless, in order to satisfy both your command and the requests of the author himself, I have rendered the whole little work in briefer, though not fewer, sentences, and, attending to accents, have brought it as far as I could into my own manner and style of writing. I kept the order and material of the earlier volume, but completely changed the form and customary mode of expression. I added many things that seemed useful to me in almost every place; I took away a few; in individual cases I altered the words, not the sense. For your command moved me to dare this, and the insistent request of the aforesaid father persuaded me. For you wished me to make a new work out of old material, to add whatever seemed suitable to me, to cut away superfluities, and to alter what had to be changed. I have done what I could; I have obeyed your commands; by rewriting it I have completed, according to the strength of my ability, which is slight, the work enjoined upon me.

Receive now, therefore, most beloved fathers, a work not mine but yours, not composed by me but rather rewritten. If it pleases you, praise the talent of the aforesaid father; but if, because of its meanness, it displeases you, correct my imperfection, since I, who had from another's resources the best material for a spiritual edifice, have through my inexperience constructed an unsuitable structure. If I have become foolish, you compelled me. Therefore, whether the work pleases or displeases, it was easier for me, by writing ineptly, to accept your command obediently than, against obedience, to keep silence. Yet I trust not in my own powers but in another's merits, since a work that charity has produced will displease no one who loves God.

I desire that your paternities may always remain happy in Christ. From Sponheim, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord's incarnation 1497.

Here begins the book On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Persons, and on their spiritual exercise.

When I call to mind the state of the monastic life in this time, I grieve deeply over its calamity, because the fervor of spiritual exercise, which once produced most abundant fruits in the order of our holy father Benedict, has now for the most part failed among monks. For we see cloistered persons returning in their morals to the world; we see the institution of regular observance despised by many; and religion, which from the beginning had been instituted for contempt of the world, is again being recalled to the vanities of the world by wicked monks. The crown has fallen from our head; the integrity of regular discipline has been corrupted; and the former fervor of holy conduct has perished. We see many monasteries of our order lying buried in the worst deformity; but we see very few reformed to the purity of the Rule.

The cause of this destruction of regular institution is negligence in spiritual exercises; for as soon as the spirit of fervor grew dull in the minds of cloistered persons, the flesh, previously dead through self-denial, revived, and the world, which before had appeared dry and contemptible to devout hearts, began to flourish again in carnal minds. Indeed, the thought of the human heart, prone to evil from youth, unless it has been stirred up to fervor of spirit by the daily bridle of spiritual exercise, soon falls back into its former negligence and grows lukewarm from its holy purpose. For just as newly broken ground, deprived of the diligent care of a cultivator, quickly returns, as thorns grow up, into its former desolation, so the human mind, however pure or holy it may be, is quickly reduced to thickets of vices unless it is renewed to fervor of spirit by the daily exercise of devotion. Led by this consideration, the fathers of our Bursfeld observance, devout cultivators, commanded us and posterity by word and example that, since because of our frailty we cannot remain steadfast in fervor of spirit, at least by an evening recollection after Compline, accusing the negligences of the day, [unclear] of the mind

[unclear] in our state, that we may be renewed to the fervor of our purpose? But whoever has neglected the exercise of daily instruction falls into a deep torpor, as the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: If you do not hold yourself steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown; and this is understood as a good conscience. The Rule of our father Benedict seems sufficient for a monk, since it is agreed to contain all the material of exercises, both spiritual and bodily, necessary for monks for the preservation of regular discipline. And therefore all the exercises of monks must be humbly subjected to the constitutions of the Rule, because whatever is prescribed either by us or by others for the instruction of monks is all assigned to the observance of the monastic norm. For the whole sum of our religion, which is acquired by the continuation of spiritual exercise, is contained in compendium, as in its root, in the Rule of monastic tradition. Therefore every exercise of monks, whether spiritual or bodily, by which the mind is led from love to a humble lowering of itself, is conformed to the ordinances of the holy Rule; and the more it is known to present a monk as good and humble, close to God, the more it opposes the studies of contemptuous pride. The holy mysteries of this exercise direct the mind of its worshippers, by an invisible teaching, toward the love of God as toward its due end along a secure path; they wondrously acquire the grace of inward devotion; and they cause the monk to despise all earthly things as nothing and to burn sweetly at all times with the lower spirit. The animal man does not receive this wholesome exercise of devotion; the vain and curious monk does not understand this study; the proud man does not admit this knowledge, to be preferred to all things. Happy is he who learns to penetrate the secrets of this exercise; happy is he who has deserved to receive this gift of holy compunction from the Lord, for whoever has once perfectly obtained it will fear no adversities of this world. But that exercise which, lacking its due end, does not direct the minds of cloistered men to the observance of the commandments of the Rule does not infuse the holy spirit of discipline, because where the obedience of subjection is despised, no gift is accepted by almighty God.

For it is written: Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to hearken is better than to offer the fat. And although many little works of spiritual exercise, composed by various persons, are found, nevertheless, because not all things suit everyone, it has seemed good to us also to publish something in conformity with the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, by which we may be able to stir ourselves up more greatly and more nearly to the purity of regular observance. Therefore we divide the present little work, collected from the exercises of the excellent father Theoderic, once abbot of the monastery of Bursfeld, into two principal parts. The first of these is set in the consideration of monastic institution; the second is occupied with the exercise of the spiritual life. In the first you are ordered to know yourself; in the second, to raise the mind from earthly things to heavenly things. Therefore, approaching according to our powers the purpose of the consideration, we divide the first treatise into three parts, according to the threefold state of cloistered men, of whom we may call the first sensual, the second rational, the third spiritual. From this threefold state of men we take a fitting title for this work, which we call On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Men. In these three regions the whole crowd of monks is included, as will be said in what follows.

On the first region of the soul, in which carnal monks dwell with beasts: disordered by many passions, living sensually in the lowest region.

The first region of the soul, therefore, is called sensual, lowest, and animal; in it are contained the roots of all evils. Men set in this dark region share with beasts according to their kind; indeed they observe, so to speak, beastly manners, while they yield either nothing or little to reason, but concede all things to sensuality like beasts. For in that lowest region three sensual powers of the soul preside. The first, the sensitive power, is diffused among the objects of the five exterior senses; the second, the concupiscible power, delights in carnal things; the third, the irascible

by fleeing the pleasures of the flesh, he pursues things contrary to them.

And this lowest region is compared to the airy heaven; for just as hailstorms, snows, lightning, and various tempests are generated in the air, so also in the minds of carnal men inhabiting this dark region various tempests of vices rage. Woe to carnal monks who inhabit this dark region, in which there is frequent motion of crimes, a continual tempest of pleasures. These are monks given over to animal passions, who subject reason to sensuality, who live according to the flesh in bestial desires. Now the works of the flesh dwelling in this lowest region are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, shamelessness, lust, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, rivalries, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these; concerning which the holy Apostle proclaims that those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God.

These are the signs of the works of the lowest region; these are the deadly tempests of the carnal minds of monks, who live irreligiously in religion, who despise the traditions of the holy fathers, who with ruinous presumption contemn the precepts of their elders. These are the unclean cultivators of the lowest region, given over to vices and carnal desires, who do not care to have God in their knowledge, who enervate themselves with the pleasures of the flesh, who stubbornly break the vow of holy religion which they professed, who, despising the salvation of their souls, disdain to follow the grace of God calling them.

Therefore he handed them over to a reprobate sense and to false judgment, so that they consider evil good, and those things which in truth are very bad they falsely judge to be very good. These are those of whom the holy Apostle prophesied: carnal monks, whisperers, detractors, hateful to God, insulting, proud, exalted, inventors of evils, disobedient to their superiors, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy, filled with all iniquity, malice, wickedness, contention, deceit, and malignity. For those who do such things are worthy of everlasting death, and not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them, and those who, from their office, in no way oppose the pursuits of the wicked.

For indeed the ruler of souls who does not correct delinquent subjects entangles himself in the crimes of others for his damnation; and by keeping silent he is made the companion of those whose faults damnation will follow. For whoever, being set as a pastor of souls, neglects to amend sinners according to canonical rule, even if he is without fault of his own, nevertheless before the strict Judge he will be condemned for another’s desert. For the supreme shepherd says to the prophet: Son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel; and you shall hear the word from my mouth and announce it to them from me. If, therefore, when I say to the wicked man, You shall die by death, you do not announce it to him, nor speak so that he may turn from his impious way and live, that wicked man indeed shall die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from your hand.

And our blessed father says in the Rule: Let the abbot know, he says, that the fault of the shepherd will lie upon him if the householder can find any lack of profit in his sheep. O sentence to be feared above all by all shepherds, by which not only the depraved conduct of subjects is ascribed to the rector, but he is also held guilty before the inward Judge for their lesser progress. O what shall we miserable shepherds say in that strict examination, we who neglect to amend according to the Rule the monks committed to us when they sin in many ways; we who do not call those lying in the lowest region to higher things, but, carnal with the carnal, grow sluggish in the shadow of death through destructive idleness.

Woe to all who remain in this dark region; for unless they do penance, they must be assigned with those who inhabit the outer darkness, where no order but perpetual horror dwells. For just as monks walking according to the rule of the spirit are to be happily crowned without end in heaven with the holy angels, so those who, contrary to the norm of monastic institution, persevere in this lowest region of the flesh until death, worse than pagans, are to be eternally tormented with demons in hell. For that blessed man truly said: Just as I have never seen men better than those who have advanced in the cenobium, so I have not experienced any worse than those who have failed in the monastery. For monastic profession requires the perfection of the spiritual life, and tends toward the summit of virtues as toward its proper due end. But insofar as anyone [unclear] from this effort of making progress in /

has failed after being placed in a monastery, by so much the farther does he withdraw from the purpose of a monk.

In what way carnal monks, citizens of this lowest region, are disordered in many articles.

Although the description of this lowest region is generally fitting for any carnal human beings who dwell in sins and crimes with beasts, nevertheless, so that we may attend to our own, we intend to speak of lukewarm and carnal cloistered men, doing no injury at all to the good and devout. For always and in all things we wish the conduct of good cloistered men to remain untouched and unharmed whenever we discuss the evil pursuits of the depraved. Therefore we rebuke evil cloistered men and depraved manners; honoring the good everywhere, as is fitting, we praise them. And what else than evil can we say of the evil, in whom we find no good things to say? In a holy order they live disorderly; they despise the traditions of the elders; they do not admit the words of salvation.

So great, indeed, is the disorder of the monks of the lowest region that, in my judgment, it would be easier to convert a publican than to recall a disorderly monk to penitence. This disorder of carnal monks we comprise in eight articles, although we are not unaware that they are disordered in many things. First, indeed, the citizens of this lowest region, beastly monks, are disordered toward God; next, toward their prelate; third, the prelate toward his subjects; fourth, the members toward one another; again, fifth, they are disordered toward themselves; then toward the goods of the monastery; seventh, toward contempt of the world; consequently, toward penitence for sin. These are the principal disorders of the citizens of the lowest region; these are the beastly affections of carnal monks, who dwell in the lowest things in mind and body, who do not hasten to advance toward the highest things. These disordered conditions of the lowest region, therefore, I shall take care to set forth briefly in order, and to demonstrate, as far as I can, how far carnal monks are from God. For, as the prophet says, salvation is far from sinners.

[unclear]

In what way the citizens of this lowest region are disordered toward God. Article I.

Therefore the carnal monks of this lowest region, mad inhabitants, are disordered toward God in many ways: they never feel the sweetness of his love; they admit no compunction of divine fear; in their affections they are beastly and swollen with pride; in their carnal pleasures they are unclean at all times.

And first, indeed, their disorder toward God takes its origin from ignorance, since, given over to animal passions, they do not care to have God in their knowledge, nor do they consent to think on those things that lead the soul to fear of him; but, blinded by evil desires, they vanish away in their thoughts. But what does Scripture say? He who is ignorant will be ignored. They do not wish to understand so that they may do good; they do not tremble before the face of the strict judge; without penitence they continually persevere in evil. Indeed, in the manner of beasts of burden, they do not fear to rot in their pleasures; they do not heed the patience of God calling them to penitence; they seek nothing other than the advantages of their flesh. At all times they walk in the greatest sins without any fear; they stubbornly refuse to know the ways of the Lord.

They think little of the future judgment, or not at all; they do not fear the punishments prepared in hell for sinners; the grace of compunction never pierces their hearts, for the love of God does not inflame their minds. They have no care for God; no dread of death. They obey the belly rather than God; at all times they desire to live according to the flesh; and [unclear] shamefully neglect their own salvation; they descend to hell with demons. Indeed, those who, forgetful of God, keep badly the vow of holy monastic life do not attain the rewards of heavenly life that are to be given to the just.

Second, carnal monks are disordered toward God by foolish profession, because they promise to live according to the Rule, yet do not truly care to fulfill this. And what is more disorderly than to promise holiness of life to the Lord God and to remain in the foulness of one’s former life? Whoever conducts himself in a monastery otherwise than the monastic Rule teaches is a mocker of almighty God, not a monk.

Because we see many today among cloistered persons living secularly; that more of them seem to neglect the purpose of their profession; that the observance of regular discipline is violated in various ways; that they knowingly ignore the goodness of God; that they refuse to do penance.

Thirdly, many cloistered persons of this lowest region are disordered toward God through neglect of the service owed to him: they serve their own affections and carnal desires in various ways, and always come to the service of God with a distracted mind. Of these, some come lukewarm to choir without any devotion; others come unwillingly, compelled by necessity; certain men, scattered by outward thoughts, are present bodily at the divine offices, but in mind wander outside through various workshops. Others do not fear to seek out false excuses by which they may, as it were lawfully, absent themselves from choir. Now they feign severe pain in the head; now they mendaciously allege this, now that; and while they deceitfully withdraw the service owed to almighty God, they incur the reproach of eternal malediction owed to the negligent.

Fourthly, there are very many disordered toward God through the working of habit: even if they sometimes escape the malediction of the negligent, nevertheless they never approach the fruit of eternal devotion. For they come to the service of God from habit alone, nor are they moved to any good work by devotion. Others, placed under grave necessity, obey the commands of superiors quite unwillingly, and fear temporal penalties rather than the judgment of God. These carry the cross of the Lord with Simon under compulsion; like the heifer of Ephraim trained for threshing, they persist in good works by habit alone. But those do not do good well who come to the service of God with an intention not duly ordered. They also perform the deed of the just without the reward of the just, who in good and just works do not take up a good will.

Fifthly, the citizens of the lowest region are disordered toward God through the vice of ingratitude, which is the greatest crime of a disordered will. And indeed, he who is found ungrateful to the Lord for benefits received is often, by his own deserving, exposed to being scourged by various and most grievous temptations. And therefore he deserves to lose the benefit that he has received, who

neglects to show to his benefactor. And what greater ingratitude can there be than not to live religiously in religion: to break a vow, to violate shamefully the purpose solemnly undertaken? For the monk who entangles himself in carnal vices, who neglects to live according to the rule which he has professed, willingly incurs the greatest vice of ingratitude.

How the monks of this lowest region are disordered toward their prelate. Article II.

Toward their prelate carnal monks are disordered in many ways: they tear apart his life with continual detractions; with a stubborn heart they disparage his pastoral office; they refuse, according to the rule, to show the affection of filial love to their pastor. For, blinded by various pleasures of the flesh, the monks of this lowest region disdain to consider whose place the abbot holds in the monastery; and him whom they ought humbly to have venerated as Christ's vicar, they regard, as though like themselves by reason of weakness, as worthy of no honor. Under the snare of this disorderly conduct, the ancient enemy deceives carnal monks, whom in various ways he brings into displeasure with their pastor. For the greatest power of raging against the monastic flock is granted to the devil when he who presides is hated by his subjects. For just as a sick man cannot be healed who, detesting the physician, does not allow him to approach, so a monk cannot be saved who, because of aversion, does not wish to disclose his temptations to his pastor. For how will a sick sheep be able to escape the teeth of the ravening wolf, if it cannot endure the presence of the shepherd?

First, therefore, disorderly monks disparage the life of their pastor, and stubbornly accuse his deeds, because when they consider that their ruler walks according to the traditions of the holy fathers, they fear to be corrected in their depravity. For among reprobate minds the life of good men is always drawn into suspicion; envy is always tormented by the virtues of others; and the monk who voluntarily subjects himself to vices and sins.

Article III.

A disorderly monk is one who attempts [unclear] against the rules of the monastery of a venerable order. And there are three ways of this: first, when a monk has had something disorderly, he ought to be excommunicated. Second, when a disorderly monk has had excommunication, they ought to be excommunicated by the same. Third, when a monk has had something disorderly, they ought to give excommunication to him. Why then? First, so that he does not give offense in what is done to himself. Second, so that he does not offend other monks. Third, so that he does not do injustice. Fourth, so that he does not do what is contrary to the good part. Fifth, so that he does not confirm error. Sixth, so that he does not abide in error. Seventh, so that he does not contribute to sins. Eighth, so that he does not summon into evil. Nineteenth, so that he does not come into the forum. Tenth, so that he does not come into the council. Eleventh, so that he does not come to the synod. Thirteenth, so that he does not come before the master. Fourteenth, so that he does not come against the custom of any bishop. Seventeenth, so that he does not come as one deputed before the pope. Sixteenth, so that he does not come to the apostolic chaplaincy. Twenty-first, so that he does not come on account of this. Twenty-third, so that he does not come for the aforesaid cause. Twenty-third, so that he does not come if he has excommunication against him. Twenty-fourth, so that he does not come except through him who had the power of excommunicating. Twenty-sixth, so that he does not come, not even if the monk is sick. Twenty-seventh, so that he does not come [unclear] of the same sickness. Twenty-ninth, so that he does not come when he is sick. Thirtieth, so that he does not come with the sick. Thirty-first, so that he does not come without apostolic license. Thirty-second, so that he does not come except at certain times. Thirty-third, so that he does not come against the ordained temporal [unclear]. Thirty-fourth, so that he does not come, contrary to the good part, in habit. Twenty-fifth, so that he does not come, being committed to sins. Twenty-eighth, so that he does not come by the custom of the church. Twenty-seventh, so that you do not come before popes. Twenty-eighth, so that you do not come to the synod. Twenty-ninth, so that you do not come before the master. Thirty-second, so that you do not come for the aforesaid cause.

Moreover, a disorderly monk is one who, against the rules of the monastery, has had [unclear], and ought to be excommunicated. And there are three ways of this: first, when a monk has had injustice, they ought to be excommunicated. Second, when a monk has had something unjust, they ought to give excommunication by the same. Third, when a monk has something unjust, they ought to give excommunication to him. Why then? First, so that he does not give offense in what is done to himself. Second, so that he does not offend other monks. Third, so that he does not do what is unjust. Fourth, so that he does not do what is contrary to the good part. Fifth, so that he does not confirm error. Sixth, so that he does not abide in error. Seventh, so that he would not tolerate sins. Eighth, so that he would not summon into evil. Nineteenth, so that he does not come to the forum. Eleventh, so that you do not come before the synod. Twelfth, so that you do not come before the master. Thirteenth, so that you do not come for the aforesaid cause.

Moreover, a disorderly monk is one who, against the rules of [unclear], has had [unclear] and ought to have excommunication. And there are three ways of this: first, when a sick monk has had [unclear], they ought to be excommunicated. Second, when a sick man has had a sick woman, they ought to give excommunication by him. Third, when a sick man has excommunication. Why then? First, so that he does not give offense in what is done to himself. Second, so that he does not offend other monks. Third, so that he does not do what is unjust to the sick. Fourth, so that he does not do what is contrary to the good part for the sick. Fifth, so that he does not confirm errors for the sick. Sixth, so that he does not abide in error for the sick. Seventh, so that he would not tolerate sins for the sick. Eighth, so that he would not summon the sick into evil. Nineteenth, so that he does not come to the forum for the sick. Eleventh, so that you do not come before the master for the sick. Thirteenth, so that he is not [unclear] before popes for the sick.

Moreover, a disorderly monk is one who, against the ordained temporal [unclear], has had [unclear] and ought to have excommunication. And there are three ways of this: first, when a monk has had [unclear] at the aforesaid time, he ought to have excommunication. Second, when he has had the aforesaid temporal [unclear], they ought to give excommunication to the same. Third, when he has the aforesaid excommunication. Why then? First, so that he does not give offense in what is done to himself. Second, so that he does not offend another monk. Third, so that he does not do what is unjust at the aforesaid times. Fourth, so that you do not do what is contrary to the good part at the aforesaid times. Fifth, so that he would not tolerate sin at the aforesaid times. Sixth, so that he would summon the aforesaid sins. Seventh, so that he confirms

[unclear]: he always hates a pastor of purified conduct.

Second, the citizens of this dark region are disorderly toward their prelate, when they disparage his office, though they are not ignorant that he has been ordained by God to preside in the monastery. On an easy occasion they murmur against him; they do not observe his commands; and those who had long ago, for love of God, subjected themselves to the arms of holy obedience now, after the manner of Sarabaites, with obedience despised, usurp for themselves the will of their own desires as a pernicious lord. They desire to have an abbot suited to their own depraved habits; they reject one who is holy and useful. If they find a lax and sluggish pastor, they intoxicate him with many poisons by flattering him, calling him the best and most pious father; and they subject themselves to him not humbly but willingly, since from him they fear no correction of their wickedness.

Third, carnal monks show themselves disorderly toward their own pastors when they withhold from them the affection of filial love and scorn to obey according to the Rule. Yet since a monk is bound to love his abbot with sincere affection as the vicar of Christ, he will not be able to hate him without very grave crime. Indeed, he who does not love his pastor for the love of Christ is not a true lover of God. For Christ, who wishes even enemies to be loved, how would he permit his own vicars to be hated? Therefore consider him who wished an abbot to be set over you in his own stead, and henceforth there will be no cause of displeasure against him.

Fourth, the disorderly citizens of the shadowy valley derogate from reverence for their pastor, when they not only disdain to render him the honor due by the Rule, but, what is worse, do not even fear to inflict insult upon him. For the Rule declares that the abbot holds the place of Christ in the monastery, and all monks ought humbly to obey him as Christ himself, since the obedience that is rendered to superiors is shown to Christ. But perverse cloisterers, always ungrateful for the precedence of their prelates, do not fear contumaciously to oppose the divine ordinance; they disdain to obey the commands of the holy Rule; and they dishonor their abbot, to whom they ought to show all reverence, tearing him with hatred and detraction. Whatever he does, whatever he ordains, whatever he has said, it displeases them as badly done, since at all times they detract from his way of life; despising his office, these diseased sheep seek nothing more than the confusion of their pastor. Some of these judge and despise their abbot in secret; others contradict him to his face; and while they neglect to show reverence to their pastor, they throw all observance of discipline into confusion. Pride is always familiar to them, and shamefulness friendly to the flesh, since those who voluntarily withdraw themselves from the affection of their pastor fall into abominable temptations and the worst crimes. For whoever despises the vicar of Christ in the monastery hands over to the devil the power of raging against himself, and confounds the unity of the mystical body.

Fifth, carnal monks, disorderly toward their pastor, disparage his authority when they think that nothing is permitted to him in the cenobium unless they themselves have consented. With haughty neck they despise the virtue of humility; they spurn regular subjection; they disdain to yield to their betters. They wish to thrust themselves into all business and cases, and to usurp for themselves the primacy of counsel, so that the abbot may dare to do or arrange nothing unless the matter first proceeds by their consent. But what does the blessed legislator Benedict say in the Rule? “The abbot, having heard the counsel of the brothers, should consider it with himself and do what he judges more useful.” And again: “Let the brothers give counsel with all the subjection of humility, so that they do not presume insolently to defend what has seemed good to them; rather, let it depend on the abbot’s judgment, so that all may obey what he has judged to be more salutary.” And again, concerning the ordaining of a prior, he says: “We have provided that, for the sake of preserving charity and peace, the ordering of his monastery should depend on the abbot’s decision.” This ordinance certainly concerns the appointment and removal of all officials of the monastery; it requires not the consent of the brothers but the counsel of those who fear God. Finally, the Rule commands that everything be done according to the will of the abbot, and that absolutely nothing be presumed that has not been enjoined by him. This authority of his, carnal monks, rash usurpers of their own will, by various

[Unclear] he tries to break, and to disturb the order and charity of the whole monastery, while they think that nothing should be done by the ruler except what they themselves think right. But tell me, proud inhabitants of the lowest region, who always establish your own will, who usurp another’s right for yourselves: is this the virtue of obedience, to refuse to yield to the command of a superior, but to cling stubbornly to your own judgment? The holy father did not prescribe in the Rule that you should live thus; he commanded you in all things to follow the will of the abbot. For obedience is the greatest virtue of a monk, which our divine father wished to commend so highly that he said a good work done without the abbot’s will lacks merit. Hence, giving instruction, he concludes thus: therefore let all things be done with the abbot’s will, and let no one in the monastery follow the will of his own heart. But if the ruler’s prudence does not seem sufficient for the ordering of the monastery, that must be imputed to the carnal monks, who voluntarily set over themselves one who was unsuitable. Folly always hates prudence, and wicked monks detest a wise abbot. Those, therefore, who knowingly set a fool over themselves will necessarily be subject to his ordering and will. Finally, no insufficiency of the shepherd ought to extinguish the obedience of subjects, since the Rule commands us to obey even one who is useless. For it says: the abbot’s commands must be obeyed in all things, even if he himself, which God forbid, acts otherwise. But when we rebuke disobedience, carnal monks object: “We do these things rightly and with good intention, since we see the substance of the monastery perishing through bad governance.” But the Apostle contradicts you, because evils must not be done so that good things may come; nor, on account of loss in a temporal matter, is the subjection of humility to be abandoned. For when a choice arises between undergoing some loss of temporal substance and danger to regular obedience, it is better for the substance to perish than for the purity of obedience to be harmed. For God will not require monies from our hands, but souls. Indeed, whoever prefers [unclear] to obedience [unclear]. But the citizens of this lowest region, carnal monks, tear apart the virtue of obedience in various ways and attack the weapons of holy humility, so that it seems easier to me to train a new monk from the world than to be able to amend the sloth of these men. But from their fruits we plainly know what sort they are: namely, those who violate peace and charity in the monastery, disturb the concord of unity, sow discord between the brothers and the abbot, and stubbornly refuse to obey the commands of the Rule. These are the works of bad cloisterers; these are the signs of the lowest citizens, who, as most wicked defenders of their own will, cast away the weapons of holy obedience, live by the flesh and not by the spirit, defer either not at all or only slightly to the statutes of the fathers, and do not acquiesce in sound counsels; their condemnation is just. For just as it is impossible for a blazing fire not to rise upward, so it is impossible for a monk without obedience to penetrate the secrets of heaven.

How the shepherds of this lowest region are disordered toward their subjects. Article III.

Since we have shown that many monks of the lowest region are disordered toward their shepherds, shall we, as though sparing ourselves, not show the disorders of prelates toward their subjects? Neither does the name of abbot sanctify anyone, nor does the eminence of pastoral care save an undeserving man. Therefore, since many among the prelates inhabit the mountain of the lowest region with the beasts of the earth, they are by no means to be passed over by us in silence. For many rulers of cloistered men show themselves disordered toward their subjects: they not only neglect to feed according to the Rule the souls entrusted to them, but tear and kill them in various ways. But whenever anyone from the lowest region is taken up as a shepherd, the pursuits of the wicked are strengthened for the worse. Therefore a good man who loves God must be promoted as abbot: one who has long since overcome this lowest region, who has learned how to tame the passions of the flesh, who both wills and is able to ascend to that highest region of the spirit. For the abbot of monks must be of higher merit than the monks, since whoever is established as a ruler of souls:

it is necessary that he be adorned with many virtues. For if a pastor, still weak, dwells in the lowest region with the sheep, by neglecting the feeble he kills them, he does not strengthen them. For if a blind man offers guidance to a blind man, he must fall into the pit together with him. But the pastor who does not show himself ordered toward his subjects according to the Rule is to be called not a pastor but a hireling, and he will not remain forever in the house of the Lord. There are, moreover, many disorders of carnal prelates, which do the more harm the more rarely they are corrected.

And first, indeed, a ruler is disordered toward his subjects if he is a hireling: if, neglecting the sheep, he seeks his own advantage of flesh or soul; if, so that he may be able to achieve his own will, he refuses nothing to those who ask things contrary to the Rule. For indeed one who is a hireling does not truly love the sheep: he seeks his own glory; he desires to be over others; he does not care to benefit them according to the Rule; he rejoices to be called abbot; he does not know how to show himself a pastor. Therefore he receives the vain reward of his vanity, who seeks not God's glory but his own; who would sooner allow the souls of his subjects to perish than resign the abbacy to a better man. He is a hireling, and the sheep do not belong to him. He is not a true monk, he is not a good pastor, he is not a sincere lover of God, who, while presiding over monks, is unwilling to yield if by the counsel of those who fear God it has seemed expedient. The care of governing souls rejects a proud man; it requires one humble and resigned to God in all things. Therefore, if you wish to be found a good pastor and a true monk, remember that your intention must at all times be formed in such a way that you are prepared, out of love of God, humbly to feed according to your powers the souls committed to you; and that you are prepared also to resign the pastoral office, at the judgment of God and of good men, from integrity of heart. If you always preserve this intention abiding in your mind, you will be a good pastor both to yourself and to others. But if in the pastoral care you love your own honor; if you prefer your advantage to the benefit of your subjects, you still dwell with the beasts in the lowest region, and you make manifest that you are of a disordered heart.

Secondly, a pastor of souls becomes disordered toward his subjects if his mind is occupied too greedily with temporal affairs; if he bears greater anxiety for secular business than for the souls committed to him. This excessive care for temporal things the holy father Benedict forbids in the Rule, and he rightly judges rational souls to be preferred to all the things of the world. "Before all things," he says, "let the abbot not, by dissembling or slighting the salvation of the souls committed to him, bear more anxiety for transitory, earthly, and perishable things; but let him always consider that he has undertaken to rule souls, for which he is to render an account." Thereupon the loving father gives assurance concerning bodily necessities, if one who loves God worships him with a pure mind. "And lest perhaps," he says, "he complain of smaller resources, let him remember what is written: First seek the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things will be added to you. And again: Nothing is lacking to those who fear God."

But the disordered pastor of monks is seduced by greed; he is blinded in mind as though without feeling; having cast away from himself the fear of the Lord, sold under sin with Ahab, he runs to the aid of wickedness; he [sets aside?] confidence in the promises made through the holy father about obtaining necessities; he is occupied with external things more than befits a monk. Driven thereafter by the goads of greed, he despises the commandments of God and of holy mother Church; he does not keep feast days; he is wholly immersed in earthly affairs; he meditates on nothing other than temporal things. Like Saul, the fool transgresses the commandment of God; in his folly he thinks that he is expiated by sacrifices against obedience. Finally, grown fat and enlarged either by secular affairs or by secular cares, he very often falls into every wantonness and dissolution; he detests the observance of regular discipline; and while he fears being restrained from evil pursuits by the authority of the chapter, he seeks the dissolution of the holy union. Then, having become reprobate with Saul, he invokes the counsel of the pythoness; he declares obedience to reform damnable for his monastery; he desires to be absolved as quickly as possible from submission to the holy confederation; to this end he relates many things falsely and mendaciously. But when the authority of the annual chapter is despised with impunity, there remains

so that monastic observance is wrecked; for the love of God keeps the good regularly in discipline, and the fear of correction restrains the wicked from evil works. Whoever, however, strives to evade the unity of the chapter imitates the devil. Thus the emperor of the Bulgarians orders the Christians subject to him to hold an assembly in church, under [unclear], though he grants them freedom to believe whatever they wish. For that crafty man knew that the sincerity of the Christian faith could not long stand, if the office of public exhortation should happen to be lacking. This adversary of the Christian faith the disorderly and carnal abbot strives as far as he can to imitate, when he resists the founding of so necessary a chapter. For the authority of the chapter alone is what maintains the observance of regular discipline in the order; and if it is despised, no integrity of monastic life will remain.

But the inhabitant of the lowest region, the disorderly abbot, devises countless pretexts against regular observance: he mentions the conditions of his monastery as contrary; he complains that his ancient privileges are [unclear]; he is indignant that his subject monks are [unclear]. But woe to disorderly men, through whom it shall happen that even one monastery is lost from this most holy congregation.

Next, the plague of avarice makes an abbot not only disorderly toward his subjects, but also opposed to himself and wholly turned away from God. For cupidity is the root of all evils; it takes away the servant of Christ and makes him a minister of the devil. Therefore the abbot who has submitted his mind to this vice shows himself to be not a shepherd but a hireling. He always gapes after earthly gains; he cares nothing for the progress of souls. A book of sacred reading is rarely or never seen in his hands; registers of revenues are more often turned over. He joins field to field; always burying gold and silver in his chest, he heaps it up; and while he too much desires his monastery to abound in temporal goods, he prepares prey for robbers. Often the public fisc of the lord [unclear] swallows and devours the monastery’s money, which the excessive greed of the monks of the monastery brings in.

Woe to you, greedy shepherd of cloistered men, who bear greater solicitude for brute animals than for the souls entrusted to you. A horse falls ill and at once you prepare a remedy; a soul perishes and you think no danger threatens. An ox and an ass are sick and you have compassion; a brother is swallowed up by sadness and you do not come to his aid. You, therefore, hireling and not shepherd, who with a stubborn heart despise the infirmities of your brothers, who do not succor those placed in bitterness, do not presume that you can escape the hand of the Lord, whose sheep you allow to perish so wickedly.

Third, a ruler is disorderly toward his subjects when those whom he ought to have guarded carefully within the enclosure of the monastery he places outside, not without danger. For indeed, when a weak monk is exposed to the governance of nuns or to secular churches, the integrity of regular observance is violated, because one who, still remaining in the lowest region, has not learned to subject the flesh to the spirit neither knows how to preside over others without danger to himself. But the disorderly shepherd who, for the sake of the advantage of temporal property, does not fear to expose his monks to so great a danger is guilty of all the souls that perish on such an occasion, and before the inward Judge he is bound to restitution for all. It does not belong to the profession of a monk to rule secular churches; it is not expedient for a weak monk to preside over nuns.

But what then? Ought a monk to set himself against the command of his shepherd if he wishes him to reside with nuns or in the churches of seculars? For the Rule commands that nothing is to be preferred to obedience. I truly do not know what I should answer to this question, so that I may not incur the danger that is seen to threaten on both sides. For if I speak the truth, I shall seem to infringe the obedience of subjection; if I consent to exposing monks to danger, I confess that I sin. Yet I shall say in a few words what I think, although I am not ignorant that truth will bring forth hatred. Just as a monk, by the necessity of his profession, is bound simply to obey his shepherd in all things that are according to the monastic rule, so a prelate cannot, without the monk’s own will, compel a monk to those things that are above the rule, especially when danger to salvation intervenes. But to rule churches, to preside over women, to reside outside the monastery: this is not to have obeyed according to the Rule. Therefore, fathers, do not [unclear] against me if I have spoken the truth; do not

to draw away, if I have expressed what seems to me: nevertheless you will do what seems to you, even if I protest. Yet truly, I beg you, do not expose your monks to chastity’s peril; do not violently compel anyone to the government of nuns and parish churches, since you can find many who ambitiously seek these offices. Obedience is indeed good, but it is by no means to be preferred to truth and the salvation of the soul. For when the danger of salvation is at issue, it is better humbly to set obedience aside by making excuse than to suffer shipwreck of chastity. Woe to the prelates of monks who incorporate churches of secular clergy into their monasteries, who loosen the bosom of desire with the torches of avarice, because, while they think they are benefiting posterity, they damn many by the occasion.

Fourth, the ruler of monks is made disorderly toward his subjects if he is found turbulent and anxious. In a pastor of souls, pious and prudent discretion is very necessary, lest either zeal for discipline be excessive or the measure of compassion be relaxed by too much laxity. But a disorderly ruler sometimes, through indiscreet fury, thinks himself the tyrant of monks; he does not know himself as father and companion of the humble. What in government is more savage, what more wicked in power, where neither God, nor reason, nor understanding, but a beast, holds rule? Truly, where God and understanding govern authority, the judgments of those presiding do not depart from the rectitude of the law of nature. But a disorderly and anxious ruler is infected by various passions of beasts; he always suspects evil of the monks, and while he wrongly directs the manner of rule, he is always anxious and fears, with Herod, to lose his kingdom.

Fifth, the pastor of cloistered men is called disorderly toward the monks if, in distributing the goods of the monastery, he is regarded as either excessive or obstinate. He is to be called excessive if, in distributing, he has been prodigal, or too diffuse in indiscreet largesse. But he is called obstinate if he has not given at the proper time the things that ought to be given, or if he grudgingly expends necessary things on his subjects. He is also to be called obstinate who casts aside the fear of the Lord, who trusts too much in his own judgment, who admits no counsels of the wise in any matters to be done. And indeed among pastors of souls there are very many disorderly through this sickness of mind, who either distribute the goods of the monastery too improvidently or preserve them with too much tenacity. They prepare most lavish banquets for their flatterers; but to others, toward whom they are averse, they refuse even the least things. In the house of guests or in their abbey, pastors, depraved by disorderly conduct and even to the point of gluttony, sometimes eat; they always drink of the best wine; but to poor monks, who by watching and singing bear the burden of the day and the heat, they scarcely grant scant necessities.

Sixth, the prelate of monks is shown to be very disorderly if, bold against God, by making little of his judgments, he is lifted up into pride. For truly, since a pastor cannot be corrected by his subjects, he is referred by the holy father Benedict to the judgment of God, as is contained in many places of the Rule. “Let the abbot know,” he says, “that concerning all his judgments he must render account to God.” And again: “But the ordained abbot should always consider what a burden he has undertaken, and to whom he is going to render account of his stewardship.” And again he says: “As soon as vices begin to arise, let him cut them off with charity, not with tyranny.” And in another place he warns, saying: “Yet the abbot himself should do all things with the fear of God and observance of the holy Rule, knowing beyond doubt that concerning all his judgments he will render account to God, the most just judge.” But the disorderly ruler of monks, like an asp with stopped ears, scorns to hear this warning of the most holy lawgiver; he despises the patience of God’s long-suffering; he thinks nothing of the future examination, until at last the angry judge says to his face: “You did these things, and I kept silence. Now, therefore, render account of your stewardship; resign to me the sheep of my inheritance, and without delay restore to me the souls once entrusted to you in the body; replace their number whole. If even one of them has perished through your negligence, my face [unclear] your soul forever

will not see. What then will you answer to the supreme shepherd, useless ruler, when not only the blood of those perishing is required of you, but also an account of those making less progress is demanded? Behold, now in the worst security, disregarding God’s judgment, you walk about; you think that everything that pleases you in the body is permitted to you, and you do not ever consider to whom you will have to render account for all things. Soon the Lord of all will come, to whom you do not fear to show yourself an unfaithful servant, whose honor you do not fear to arrogate to yourself. Unless meanwhile you do penance, unless you amend your life for the better, you will burn with demons in hell without end.

Seventh, it happens that a shepherd is disordered toward his subjects if, neglecting the common good, he seeks his own advantage with a vicious intention; if, presiding in a monastery, he serves not God but his own interests, while he rejoices that he is prelate in order to obtain the pernicious liberties of the flesh, and fraudulently provides for himself for the future from the goods of the monastery. This disorder, however, is especially seen in those who resign their office on whatever pretext; to them, as the reward of their stewardship, as if they had been bishops, an annual pension is assigned from the goods of the monastery. This is not the manner of those seeking the Lord; this is not the way of the old monks. When you resign the pastoral office for God’s sake, resign it simply; do not demand anything beyond food and clothing, if you do not wish to sin with proprietors. You are a monk; you were a monk before you became abbot; you will remain a monk after the office. Why then should you demand a pension, when you know that you are a monk? Just as in buying prelacies the vice of simony is committed, so by demanding a pension for the resignation of an abbacy one sins against the rule. What then? Do we condemn those who, resigning the office of pastoral care without fault, have received annual provisions from the goods of the monastery? Far from it. We do not forbid necessities; we deny superfluities. Yet he who is a true monk and lover of God is content with regular provision even after an abbacy.

In what ways the monks, citizens of the lowest region, are disordered toward one another.

Article Four.

The citizens of the lowest region, monks and carnal men, are disordered toward one another in many and various ways; for since, stirred up by animal passions like beasts, they do not direct themselves according to the right judgment of reason, it is no wonder if they pervert the order of brotherly life. For a troubled conscience is always savage and presumptuous, and an evil mind never has the joys of peace, but is continually shaken by vice and sorrow; it is inwardly tormented by the everlasting fires of crimes. And so monks, citizens of the dark region, blinded by evil and disordered affections, do not consider the end of the monastic profession; they love nothing but the advantage of the present life; they neglect their own salvation; they do not rise up to the love of eternity.

First, therefore, they are greatly disordered toward one another when they cast aside the intellectual regard that ought to be had among brothers; when they do not notice the image of God in man; when they do not think of the communion of grace and glory infused into men and to be granted in the future; nor do they care to show one another the love of brotherly fellowship. They live with one another like horse and mule, concordant in bodily appearance, because whatever is pleasing to sensuality they love, and whatever accords with reason they do not admit. One is loved by another not because he is a man, but because he is like his lover in the affection of sensuality. For the carnal man loves in man not virtues, not religion, not, finally, nature itself, but flesh, blood, bodily quality. Since, therefore, the love of carnal men is carnal, it is easily changeable by occasion. For the citizens of this lowest region venerate similar ways of life, and monks always embrace monks like themselves with affection. The one whom God loved from eternity the disordered cenobite persecutes; the one whom God, because of his demerits, despises, this man venerates as a saint.

Second, cloistered men are disordered toward one another by reason of dissimilarity, when either the seniors, stirred up by harshness and pride, despise their juniors, or the juniors contumaciously set themselves against their seniors. And this disorder is proved to be very contrary to the holy rule, which commands seniors to love juniors with fatherly affection, and juniors

[unclear] begins humbly to obey his seniors for God's sake. But when the seniors, citizens of this lowest region, withdraw paternal affection from the younger men, the lesser ones are inflamed with grave hatred; and when the young consider that they are unjustly despised by them, they daily accuse their corrupt morals. Therefore weak young men learn the seniors' morals, which are not upright; and, as it is said in the proverb, just as they see the elders sing, so too the younger ones dance.

Thirdly, monks are badly ordered toward one another when they cast aside good zeal and mutual obedience, and assume the evil kind of zeal that is forbidden by the Rule. By words and deeds they commit various wrongs against one another; each, in his eagerness to rival the other, strives to watch him for evil; one is provoked by another to inflict insult. They mutually reproach one another with their infirmities; they always pant for revenge. Zeal for regular discipline is despised; the passion of indignation and bitterness rules. They meet one another with averted faces, and by open signs they reveal how much hatred lies hidden in the breast. Not so the wicked, not so; for whoever persecutes his brother with hatred is proved a murderer and unworthy of the kingdom of God. O ever-wretched condition of carnal monks, which is as near to hell as it is estranged from the fear of God. For they imitate not angels but demons, all those who, through evil zeal, delight to be discordant in the school of peace. Indeed, just as a brute animal does not abandon the savagery of its nature, so a beastly monk does not withdraw from the worst zeal.

In What Manner the Monks, Citizens of the Lowest Region, Are Ordered Toward Themselves. Article V.

The carnal monks, citizens of the lowest region, are disordered in nothing more than toward themselves. For they cast aside every consideration of themselves; they do not attend to the end for which they were created; for while each one pollutes himself with the filth of vices, his wicked mind departs from the original rectitude of his condition. Nor is it any wonder if the cultivator of the lowest region becomes outwardly disordered toward others, when through various passions of the flesh he is inwardly confounded and dissipated from himself. For Scripture says: He who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good? The right order of the human condition established that the flesh should be subject to the spirit; the spirit is commanded to be subject to him from whom it received the form of being. But among carnal minds the order of reason is perverted, when the flesh rules over the spirit, and reason, which according to the power of understanding implanted in it ought to have governed all things, being suffocated by the pleasures of the flesh, does not hasten under command to the rectitude of judgment.

Therefore carnal monks are disordered toward themselves through the vice of curiosity, because by inquiring into another's life they judge curiously, and do not amend their own life, defiled by every vice. They do not know how to correct great crimes in themselves, yet they proudly rebuke others who offend in very small matters. They carefully consider the speck in their brother's eye, and excuse the beam clinging to their own eyes as if it were nothing. They subject all their affections to sensuality, and, after despising the judgment of right reason, they live carnally like beasts; passion frequently stirs them to anger; the frenzy of envy inflames them against their neighbor. With an anxious mind they always demand vengeance against their brothers; often, blinded by excessive fury, they obtain it not without harm to themselves. But disordered citizens cannot long lie hidden in secret; for the more they remain unknown to themselves through the elation of the mind, the more, through blind judgment, they become manifest to others. For every proud and disordered man is said first to be ignorant of himself, because if he truly knew himself, he would by no means be proud. But since the disordering of oneself takes its origin from pride, we cannot describe this plague better than if we take care to lay open its roots, descending by degrees to the depths below. For just as the summit of the spiritual life is contained in the twelve degrees of humility, so the source of all monastic disorder is contained in the twice-six degrees of pride.

Thus the first degree of pride is called curiosity. By it monks badly ordered toward themselves neglect their own life and morals, and continually inquire into either the deeds or the words of others. At all times they accuse the negligences of the brothers; they rebuke the life of the pastor; and the more curiously they desire to know outwardly what belongs to others, the farther they withdraw from themselves. But for monks the vice of curiosity

it is most pernicious: for once it has invaded his mind, stripping him of all virtues, it makes him a dwelling-place of vices. It is a very true sign of weakness to examine the deeds of others and, beyond the rule of one’s office, to be occupied with matters belonging to others [unclear]. For the monk who, according to the definition of his name, is commanded to care for himself alone, scrutinizes the deeds of others not without manifest danger to his own salvation. But whoever subject themselves to the vice of curiosity soon descend to the second degree of pride. For one always disposes toward another, and no single sin alone rules over proud monks.

The second degree of pride, therefore, is lightness of mind and the unstable occupation of a wandering heart. Carnal monks fall into this degree of disordered conduct through various affections, which they have sensually contracted from the vice of curiosity. But the true cenobite must remain steadfast in his holy purpose, because when lightness of mind is admitted, the constancy of virtue is dissipated in the heart. It is the judgment of a disordered mind to run about through various images of things and always to produce new forms of sensual affections.

The third degree of pride is called empty joy, which is produced from the lightness of a disordered man’s mind. Carnal monks compose for themselves various images of affections; when these meet agreeably with sensuality they rejoice, but when otherwise happens, contracting grave indignation, they slip into various temptations. But that is not true joy which [unclear], nor does the gladness long continue which does not have its source in the love of God. And therefore disordered men, tossed by vain joy into boastful vaunting, fall, when they falsely ascribe great things to themselves.

The fourth degree of pride, then, as we have said, arises from empty joy; it is called foolish boasting. Carnal monks fall into this when, magnifying themselves before others, they exalt themselves. If they have done any good, they boldly bring it forward in public, often mendaciously inventing even things they have not done. They desire to seem holy, learned, prudent, and noble, and they devise many things by the craftiness of their wit, so that they may appear glorious outwardly to men, though inwardly they know they are empty of the merit of virtue. If you begin to praise anyone in their presence, they at once rise up to the contrary; they say many vicious things against him, because, while they desire to show themselves alone praiseworthy, they do not permit anyone else to be praised in their presence.

The fifth degree of pride is understood as singularity, which is generated from the swelling of vaunting. Into this degree proud cloistered men fall, who through boasting have presumed that they surpass others either in merit or in knowledge. Hence, lest they appear like the rest in their manner of life, out of self-pride alone they show themselves singular in all things. But this singularity is reprehended in the monastery, where all are commanded to live in common according to the rule. Proud monks, as blessed Bernard testifies, while they prefer themselves to others in virtues and wisdom, fall into such arrogance of rashness that they flatter themselves more over one fast while the rest are eating than if they had fasted seven other days. In short, one little prayer said singularly seems more advantageous to them than the whole psalmody of one night. During the meal they often carry their eyes around the table, and if they see someone eating less they groan and begin to grieve that they themselves have been beaten, cruelly withholding from themselves what they had provided for necessary nourishment. These proud cloistered men are energetic for their own singular practices, sluggish for common ones. In bed they keep watch; in choir and at the regular reading they drowse.

The sixth degree of pride takes its beginning from the fifth; it is called the arrogance of the proud. Indeed, when disordered cloistered men begin, through zeal for singularity, to appear outwardly to others, they burn into a greater madness of arrogance, and whatever is said by men in their praise they foolishly judge to be true. O pitiable folly of the proud: although in all other matters they believe no one more than themselves, about themselves alone they believe themselves less than another. Whatever praise of themselves they hear from the unskilled, they ascribe not to the ignorance or good will of the one praising, but to their own merits. But whoever is delightfully fed by human praises is held before the Lord to be empty of every virtue and full of arrogance.

The seventh degree of pride is born from the preceding one; it is called the presumption of the proud. This [unclear] all the arrogant

as do those who, in a singular way, believe themselves to be something great. Of these Bernard says: “He who thinks that he surpasses others, how should he not presume more concerning himself than concerning others? He sits first in the assembly; in councils he answers first; uncalled, he comes forward; unbidden, he thrusts himself in; when a matter has been arranged, he rejects what has been done by others. Whatever he himself has not done or arranged, he thinks has not been rightly done nor finely ordered. He judges those who judge; he prejudges those who are to judge. For the man for whom God is not sufficient in his heart seeks comfort in external things in vain.”

The eighth degree of pride is called the defense of sins, which indeed is always born of presumption. For a presumptuous monk always thinks himself better than everyone; if he has committed anything, he either stubbornly denies it, or, if he has been convicted, excuses it in many ways. For how will he be able humbly to confess his fault, who does not recognize himself as guilty? If you try to chastise such a man for his offenses, you always make him worse. Therefore whoever, when corrected for any matter, slips into words of malice; whoever opposes excuses for sins to the one reproving him, falls into this descent of death, opposed to the fifth degree of humility. But the presumptuous man strives to excuse his sin in various ways, for he is found to have fallen into this degree of pride. For either he says, “I did not do it”; or, “I did it indeed, but I did well”; or, if badly, “not very badly”; or, if very badly, “not with evil intention.” And if he has been convicted of malice, immediately, in excuse of himself, he does not fear to bring forward another’s counsel to the abbot, and never according to the Rule will he reveal hidden things to the abbot. But when he comes to confession, he will cloak the truth with a feigned mind, because, so that he himself may be able to escape confusion, he strives to bring others’ negligences into the open. Inwardly disordered, proud, and presumptuous, in confession he cloaks his own faults and confesses those of others. Always restless within himself, with one sentence he condemns the deeds and examinations of others; he complains that no one lives rightly in the monastery; he thinks that there is no charity among the brothers. But if his vain presumption has been detected through the skill of the confessor, he immediately seeks another confessor; and if the abbot should begin gently to wish to oppose him, the monk, lifted up into the ninth degree of pride, falls through restlessness of mind.

The ninth degree of pride is described as murmuring or impatience, which for the most part dominates carnal monks. Indeed, the man whose confession is feigned, when touched by one light insult or penance, is immediately raised up into open pride; the deceit of simulated humility is uncovered, nor can the feigned mind hide itself any longer, but it is compelled to bring out in public whatever lies hidden within. Thereafter, having become no longer in control of himself, the proud monk murmurs at everything; he obstinately accuses the shepherd’s judgment, however just; he gnashes his teeth; when stirred, he grows angry; without reason, like a madman, he is troubled by whatever he wishes. But the proud monk, given over to murmuring, having despised the fourth degree of humility, falls into the tenth descent of pride, through which he runs toward hell.

The tenth degree of pride follows murmuring, and is called rebellion. Proud and carnal monks fall into this, who, still dwelling in the lowest region, devote themselves to murmurings. Hence Bernard says: “Unless divine compassion looks upon the murmurer, so that at last, converted, he silently acquiesces in others’ judgments, which is very difficult for such men, he will soon, having become brazen and shameless, fall all the worse into this degree, inasmuch as the desperate temper of his mind does not [unclear]. He always advances toward worse things; and he who before had arrogantly despised his brothers in secret now also, what is more serious, openly shows that he despises his master.” But the censure of divine judgment does not allow this degree of pride to pass long unpunished, since monks rebellious against their shepherds frequently apostatize from the order; others, on account of serious crimes, foul prisons; some, expelled from monasteries, wander in exile, homeless and wretched; many, horribly struck by the Lord and despairing, hasten to the lower regions. For it is written: “He who resists authority opposes God’s ordinance.”

And again the Lord says of the prelates of the faithful: “He who despises you despises me.” What will you say to these things, rebellious monks? Will you cite laws to me? How long will you corrupt the truth? But I dare to say what I wish you were ashamed to hear. In the strict judgment of God, rebellious monk, presumption of law will not save you, who now proudly scorn the obedience of subjection. Law commands obedience; it requires humble subjection within order.

Consequently rebellious monks fall into the eleventh degree of pride, which is the liberty of sinning: they scorn not only the corrections and exhortations of the brethren, but also those of the prelates. For truly, when rebellion is taken up against the teacher, boldness in sinning is produced, since he who despises the authority of correction already commits all crimes as though lawfully. Love of God voluntarily restrains good cenobites from sins, and fear holds back the weak. But where neither love of God nor fear of correction penetrates the monk, then the mind, through rebellion and the habit of sinning, draws near to hell. For Scripture says: “When the wicked man has come into the depth of evils, he despises.” What does he despise? He despises God; he scorns men; in despair, he does not know how to seek the salvation of his soul.

They fall, therefore, into the twelfth degree of pride who through boldness in sinning run into evil habit. This is the nearest descent to hell; this is the path of hell; this is the swift way to the region covered with the darkness of death. Whoever has once fallen into this degree of the habit of sinning rises again only by the strong hand of God’s compassion, because when habit is not resisted, a necessity of sinning is produced. For wickedness always advances toward the worse, and, always falling, falls more deeply.

Behold, these are the twelve degrees of pride by which one descends to hell; whoever desires to escape them should always strive to keep himself in the observance of humility. In these twelve evils every unworthiness of vices darkens the cenobite, makes him disordered toward himself, and in morals changes the man into a very savage beast. The end of these things is destruction; and unless before the death of the flesh the remedy of penitence intervenes, the progress of the evil degrees damns the monk who will burn without [unclear].

Whoever, being disordered toward himself, has once fallen first into the degree of pride, if he does not strive to rise as quickly as possible through penitence, soon casts himself headlong into the second and consequently into all the rest in order. But the disorder of carnal monks toward themselves is expressed in sum in these degrees of elation, by which they are shown to be citizens of the lowest region. What, however, is said of disordered and proud monks, we must also understand of prelates of the lowest region.

In what way the citizen of the lowest region [unclear]. Article VI

Whoever, established in a monastery, neglects to order his inner affections toward the purity of holy [unclear], frequently also transgresses enormously in outward matters. Monks disordered toward God are consequently proved to be disordered toward all things. For just as the good cenobite, united by love to the divine will, considers all secondary things in the right order of reason with a simple eye, so one turned away from God through disordered affections sins even in the goods that he uses badly. Therefore carnal monks, cultivators of the lowest region, are badly disordered not only toward the soul but also toward the temporal substance of the monastery. For an outward disturbance of the body follows the inward confusion of the mind, and the one demonstrates the other.

First, indeed, the citizen of the lowest region is badly ordered toward the goods of the monastery when they demand that these be granted to them in an improper order, or in any way usurp more than the use of the regular institution permits. For the Rule commands that all necessary things be given to the monks; it utterly forbids superfluities.

Second, those use the goods of the monastery badly who do not fear to give and receive contrary to the master’s prohibition, or who faithlessly commit deceit and fraud in things entrusted to them. For a monk who, according to his own whim, without reasonable cause, contrary to the Rule, in any way without permission squanders the goods of the monastery.

against the rule, just as an unfaithful and falsifying proprietor sins.

Third, disorderly monks or abbots misuse the goods of the monastery when they indulge them in unlawful uses. Theft and sacrilege are committed together when the goods of the monastery are converted to illicit uses. For the substance of the monastery, dedicated to God, ought to be guarded like the vessels of the holy altar, lest it be dissipated in any way through negligence. But he who forbids the useless expenditure of cloistered goods would by no means, without sin, permit them to be lavished on base uses. What will the monks and rulers of the lowest region answer to the lawgiver in the strict examination, who do not fear to dissipate the goods of the monastery on parents, kinsmen, mimes, actors, and base persons, as an occasion and reward of sin?

Fourth, carnal abbots and monks sin more gravely in the goods of the monastery when they gather them too greedily, to the detriment of divine charity and of salvation. For made subject to the law of avarice, they think of nothing but profits and money; they violate feast days and do not observe them; they always desire to increase temporal goods; they do not notice the losses of charity. They grieve more over a dying beast than over a perishing sinner. So truly have all disorderly cloisterers been blinded that they consider avarice prudence and think riches to be reform. They join field to field; they call profit piety; and where they see temporal goods abound, there they say the best discipline is observed. They refuse to spend even a few things for the common good of the order, because they have truly lost the order of charity. They raise useless, curious, and damnable structures on high; they keep costly garments and ornaments scarcely necessary for divine service; they clothe sacred things with gold; they leave Christ’s poor naked. This greedy curiosity does not befit monks, since we are commanded to imitate the holy men of old and are ordered to sell these things for the support of the poor. But a covetous monk and an avaricious abbot are as far from the purpose of holy religion as the devil is from heaven.

Fifth, carnal monks sin in the goods of the monastery when they do not repay them with prayers. They all cheerfully receive the alms of the faithful, but few render the suffrages of prayers for the givers. From these things many citizens of the lowest region, when they have come to the order, serve not God but the belly; they desire that more food, drink, and clothing be given to them than necessity requires; and those who in the world could scarcely have bread and vegetables in [unclear] now, having become monks, refuse eggs and little fish. They importunately demand that great, varied, diverse, and delicate fish be given to them; murmuring through desire of the flesh with the children of Israel in the desert, they cry out for [unclear]; they say that they cannot eat eggs and peas; they always desire more delicate things.
