In what way the citizens of the lowest region are badly ordered toward contempt of the world.

Article VII.

The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it. Therefore whoever desires to enter the heavenly kingdom by the arms of holy obedience, whoever chooses to live for God under regular conversion, must do violence to the pleasures of the flesh and strongly contemn the world with all its vanities. But the carnal monks, citizens of the lowest region, who are badly ordered not only toward adverse things but also toward spiritual things, are also badly ordered toward contempt of the world.

And first, indeed, they are infected by concupiscence of the flesh, for they always burn with the fire of pleasure. In food and drink they are found excessive; in beds and baths, contrary to the rule, delicate; they prefer the desires of the flesh to the salvation of the soul; they do not seek the sweetness of inward conversation. They nourish their flesh too delicately, through which they are continually set aflame in various desires. For no one can truly contemn the world who neglects to restrain the appetite of the flesh even in the smallest things. If you eat to satiety, you do not truly contemn the world. For the first commandment imposed on those who contemn the world is grounded in abstinence alone. But if you fill your belly with food to satiety, you immediately fall either into lust or into severe sloth.

Therefore the concupiscence of the flesh draws back the mind of the disordered cenobite, so that he cannot despise the world.

Secondly, they are disordered with respect to despising the world because of the vain concupiscence of the eyes. For the monk who forgets the true honor of faithful souls delights utterly in worldly pomps and overly curious ornaments. Indeed, a person’s outward attire reveals what each one is inwardly, hidden within himself. To wear rings on the fingers, corals on neck-bands, scent-vessels in the hands, and pleats in cowls shows not a monk but a soldier; it presents not a humble cenobite but a proud secular man. This adornment in monks cannot please anyone except the reprobate; indeed, it is often found to have displeased even the proud. Woe to you, disordered cloisterers, who through the double concupiscence of the eyes descend to hell, while you desire to see in others what is not expedient, and present yourselves to be seen by others otherwise than you ought.

What have the jewels of the world to do with you? What have the curiosities of the world? All these beauties, as Saint Bernard bears witness, make a masculine soul effeminate; these public refinements quickly weaken a manly purpose. Such men are like ragged boys who, because of one thin red band fastened to a torn sleeve, think themselves very handsome and comely, and insolently mock others set before them, though very well dressed, as if they were naked. These pompous cloisterers see others walking in humble garb, despising the world in the spirit of poverty, and for that reason pleasing both God and men; but they see themselves despised by the wise and by princes, and sometimes not even admitted to conversation. Seeing these things, the proud, even if they grieve bitterly as though over an injury, nevertheless utterly refuse to lay aside their pride.

Thirdly, the citizens of the lowest region are badly ordered with respect to contempt of the world because of pride of life, since they are infected not only with vain complacencies of the flesh, but also are proud through swelling of mind. For all who follow the desires of the flesh become [unclear] in mind; they do not know how to endure equals; they do not accept superiors. They rejoice that a great retinue of servants attends them; they strive to sit in council; they always wish to appear glorious to men; they walk pompously in public. Swollen with the spirit of pride, they boast that they possess monasteries notable from their foundation, rich in temporal goods, in jewels, in buildings, and in elaborate privileges. With uplifted heart they despise poor monks or abbots of exiled monasteries; they do not blush to prefer themselves to better men. The more they desire to hunt for glory in outward things, the farther they withdraw from true glory with the foolish virgins.

How the citizens of this lowest region are disordered with respect to penance.

Article VIII.

Since man, born of woman, living a short time and filled with many miseries, cannot remain long in the same condition, it is necessary that with all zeal he turn himself, by daily reforming himself, toward his proper end, since for as long as anyone is permitted to live in this world, he is held to be changeable in either direction. Therefore whoever, placed in this mutability, desires to come to the joys of immutability should humbly acknowledge his own frailty, should always after the fall of sin flee to the remedies of penance, and should fear to lie in crime even for a moment. For the life of a monk must always consist in saving penance, and he must continually await the coming of the Judge with holy fear. For blessed Jerome says: The monk has the office not of one teaching but of one lamenting, who should mourn either himself or the world, and should fearfully await the coming of the Lord. But the disordered cloisterers of the lowest region despise this saving remedy; they consume the acceptable time in vanity; and, since they do not fear to be badly ordered in all things, they show themselves very disordered even with respect to doing penance.

First, indeed, they are badly ordered with respect to penance through carelessness of mind, while they neglect to understand how greatly sin displeases almighty God, whom they do not fear to contradict by the decision of a depraved will. Just as black night is opposed to day, so the sinner, turned away from divine goodness, is considered hostile and adversarial.

What a putrid corpse is wont to do in the sight of men, sin, in its own way, does incomparably in the sight of the angels. But carnal monks despise the honor of God, and therefore they do not notice the insult of sin. They neglect to amend venial sins, and so commit mortal sins as if with license. For Scripture says: He who neglects the smallest things falls little by little. Hence the saying of Bernard admonishes us, saying: Let no one, brothers, say in his heart, “These things are light; I do not care to correct them. It is no great matter if I remain in these venial and very small sins.” This, brothers, is impenitence; this is unforgivable blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. For no one can escape greater sins if he has despised amending the lesser. Nothing is worse than carelessness of mind.

Secondly, carnal monks, lovers of the lowest region, are exceedingly disordered with respect to penitence, since they do not notice the contagion of sin. For just as a healthy man is very often infected by a contagious disease, so from one sin a man is inclined into another. For one sin is always said to dispose toward another, unless it is amended as quickly as possible through contrition. For the prophet says: Jerusalem has sinned a sin; therefore she has become unstable; let her become filthier still. We have sufficiently shown the contagion of this disease in the degrees of pride: for just as we said that one always arises from another, so we perceive that through carelessness a man becomes slippery from one sin into another.

Thirdly, carnal monks disordered with respect to penitence contract the worst sickness through the habit of sin, while they fall into a pernicious blindness of mind. Every vice often committed is held cheap, and through habit is judged lighter. Just as grace illumines the mind, so the frequency of sin blinds reason. For it is written: Blind the heart of this people and make its ears heavy, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand, lest they be converted and I heal them, says the Lord. For when the wicked man has come into the depth of evils, he feels contempt. No sin is so great that through habit it does not seem light and small.

Fourthly, disorderly cloisterers, blinded through the habit of evil, do not come to the grace of true compunction; they approach confession superficially from habit alone; they do not abandon their depraved will; they do not truly take up the purpose of amendment. Woe to those who, buried in the habit of sin, do not fear the censure of the strict examination; who do not withdraw from blindness of mind through the remedy of contrition, since just as now they despise the long-suffering of God’s goodness, so in that terrible hour they will undergo the sentence of eternal death. What will confession of the mouth be able to profit where there is no true contrition of the heart? Without contrition there is no saving confession, nor can there be contrition without the purpose of amendment. The judgment of contrition is to be unwilling to sin any more.

Fifthly, the disorderly citizens of the lowest region, made despisers of almighty God through the habit of sinning, always fall into graver dangers of the soul, while they always approach wrongly the most holy sacred mysteries of the body and blood of the Lord. They make a superficial confession from habit; they allow themselves, thinking they are well ordered, to proceed great in their consciences. But now, as if allied with hell, they no longer fear God; they contemn the paths of an amended life; they consider themselves well ordered; they do not care with how many vices they are inwardly filled. At times, sensibly affected by a fantastic devotion, they already think that the Holy Spirit is present; they affirm that they are beloved by God and holy. They also shamelessly thrust themselves into the divine mysteries; not discerning the body and blood of the Lord, they receive it for judgment and condemnation upon themselves. Finally, such people, communicating unworthily, are more grievously hardened, because, while they think themselves very secure and to be living well, they do not duly care to cleanse their conscience from vices. Thus Judas the apostate, the evil of betrayal which before, as a certain [unclear] says, he feared to commit against the Savior, after the morsel had been taken and the devil had entered into him, did not fear to carry out boldly and without shame. O how many are the carnal monks of this lowest region, proud, arrogant, envious, murmuring, and bound fast by various sins, whose conscience is rarely or never made clean through true contrition, who nevertheless are not afraid to approach the most holy altar almost daily.

Behold how evil is the society of all in this lowest region

... of [unclear]: whose end is destruction; for whom, through the death of the body, a descent to hell is prepared. This is the far-off region, bestial and of unlikeness, into which that prodigal son went, who squandered the portion of his inheritance luxuriously with harlots. In this region dwell carnal citizens; concerning such people the holy Apostle declares: The animal man does not know the things that are of God.

In this dark region, covered with the gloom of death, no spiritual good inhabits it; in it not peace but bestial discord reigns, as the prophet says: There is no peace for the wicked, says my Lord.

Concerning those who, being near to this lowest region, more often relapse into it through inconstancy of mind.

Although between the first region of the evil and the second of the good there is, properly speaking, no middle, nevertheless there are some who often move between the two: while through weakness they are now lukewarm, now through contrition of mind they seem to be devout. These are weak human beings. Although they are not submerged in the lowest region, nevertheless through negligence they are very near it, and indeed frequently fall into it through bad habit, since they do not withdraw as far as they can from the affections of the flesh. Concerning them Bernard says in a certain sermon: Pernicious lukewarmness, because it is dangerous, because it is most troublesome and full of misery and pain, and plainly nearest to hell, is rightly reckoned the shadow of death. Indeed one may find faint-hearted and slack people, failing beneath the burden, needing rod and spurs; whose joy is brief, whose sadness is faint-hearted; whose compunction is brief and rare, since their thought is with animals, their way of life lukewarm; whose obedience is without devotion, speech without circumspection, prayer without intention of heart, reading without edification. Finally, as we see, fear of Gehenna scarcely restrains them; shame restrains them; reason scarcely bridles them; discipline scarcely holds them in check. If people of this kind remain long beneath the burden, either they are crushed and succumb, or in a certain way they are in hell, so that they never fully breathe the sweet yoke and the light burden.

And so such pernicious lukewarmness flows from this, that their will has not yet been purified, nor do they will the good as they have known it, being drawn away and enticed by their own concupiscence. For they love in their flesh little earthly consolations, whether in word or in sign or in deed or in some other thing; and if they sometimes interrupt these things, they nevertheless do not break them off completely. Hence it is that they rarely direct their affections toward God, and their compunction is not continual, but occasional. But the soul that is subject to these distractions cannot be filled with the visitations of the Lord; and the more it is emptied by those things, the more fully it will be filled with these. If much, much; if little, little. Or perhaps, if you approve this more, those things will never be able to be mixed with these for eternity. For spirit and flesh, fire and lukewarmness, do not dwell together in one house, especially since lukewarmness itself is accustomed to provoke the Lord to vomiting. Whoever, therefore, desires to flee from the midst of Babylon, whoever longs to come to the region of the spirit, should take care always to repel from himself the torpor of threatening care, and in holy purpose to burn continually through the fire of divine love. Nothing harms those who wish to serve God so much as lukewarmness of mind, which always arises at the beginning from some small negligence; but unless it is immediately cured, it increases successively and wonderfully. But one placed in the neighborhood of the lowest region often relapses into the same, because the dregs of his former carnal way of life still subtly occupy his will, and easily, on some occasion, disturb the weak fervor of devotion. But no one can rise from the depth of hell with a lukewarm will; no one can overcome a habit without a contrary habit, because unless a certain violence intervenes, habit will always strengthen the vice of sinning. This lowest region is rightly called hell, because by a certain likeness of disturbance and aversion it is compared to hell. After this life there are three dwellings of souls, which receive citizens emigrating from this world out of the three regions. For the first dwelling is called hell, and this is compared to the lowest region. For just as in hell no order, but everlasting horror, dwells, so in this lowest region all the fury of a blinded mind, affection

by carnal [unclear] it is disturbed. In hell all are evil, and in the lowest region good persons are found nowhere. But whoever fall down into hell have belonged to the lowest region. For the lowest region always sends its citizens to the lower world, unless, led by penitence, while living they have taken care to renounce dead works. The second abode is called purgatory, and this is compared to the second, rational region. For just as purgatory purges and perfects souls, and sends them, once purged, to the kingdom of heaven, so this second region washes its citizens who persevere in it, through continual exercise, from the filth of sins, and disposes them for the ascent to the third region, which is called spirit. In this abode all are good, yet still to be purged so that they may become better; and in the second region nowhere are there evil persons, yet they are always to be exercised so that they may be made better. This region sends its citizens who die in it to purgatory, since, although all are good, nevertheless they do not yet seem fit for the kingdom without a temporary purgation. Indeed, those who inhabit this middle region, although they seem to be very near the highest, nevertheless have not yet been wholly removed from the dust of the lower one. But the third abode of separated souls is called the kingdom of heaven, and this is compared to the highest region, that of spirit. For just as in that heavenly fatherland there is highest rest and eternal peace, so in the region of spirit there is continual tranquility of mind. Here ends the first region.

Preface to the second treatise of the first part, which deals with the middle region, namely the rational region of cloistered persons.

Let us now at last leave this dark region of carnal persons, in which the whirlwind of crimes remains, and the continual tempest of punishments. We have granted it enough, and we have lingered over it more than had been our purpose. Let us therefore leave the dead to bury their dead; let us yield to the darkness; let us hasten toward the light of the spiritual life. We must go out from the Egypt of the shadowy region; we must hasten diligently, through the middle region of reason, to the highest summit of spirit. Let us now, then, at last approach the middle region of the soul, through which one comes successively to the highest. This region of the soul is quite suitably called rational, in which there is continual labor for seeking out the highest truth. The fervor of mind strives always to raise the citizens of this middle region to higher things; but the weakness of the flesh, by the motion of a raging whirlwind, struggles to draw them back to the lowest things. From this arises continual labor; from this arise sighs and groans, because the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the sense that thinks many things. This is the narrow way that leads to life, and few walk through it. In this region violence is imposed upon the concupiscences of the flesh until the will is subjected to the spirit at its nod. For the Lord says in the Gospel: The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it. In this region the war of combat is declared to the servant of God; so the wise man testifies: Son, he says, when you approach the service of God, stand in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation. How great the temptations are in this middle region we learn daily through the difficulty of spiritual exercises, while, driven in various ways, we are not able to remain long in the fervor of spirit. Now the weakness of the flesh calls us back from the zeal for advancement; now the temptation of the ancient enemy vexes us; now the company of neighbors hinders us;

now the deceitfulness of the world leads astray. Therefore those who wish to make progress in this region of labor have need of the greatest courage, because no one can resist his temptations to the end unless he strives daily to do violence to himself. But whoever thinks that he has come to this region should not presume on his own powers, for just as the grace of God, in order to work the good in us, requires the choice of our will, so the will necessarily requires grace. For no one is holy by his own powers. Therefore let no one dare to presume on himself, but let him who stands take heed lest he fall. The life of man upon earth is warfare, for through many tribulations one comes to the kingdom, and heaven is acquired by the arduous labors of the virtues. “Going,” says the prophet, “they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.” Indeed, those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. But if anyone fails in the sowing, certainly he will not rejoice in the harvest. Since, therefore, through the continual labors of spiritual exercise the mind must be cleansed from the dust of the first region, do not seek leisure in this middle region; do not love the repose of negligence, because no one is able to stand here except the one who courageously girds himself for continual labor. Whoever in this middle region does not always advance toward better things soon falls into the negligences of his former life, and there incurs the danger of failing where he has lost the desire of making progress. This is the place of continual combat; whoever neglects to fight in it falls back to be conquered. The preface ends.

Begins the second region of the soul, which is called rational, in which men are occupied amid many labors. Therefore the second region of the soul is called rational, in which the mind is exercised by continual labor for the inquiry into the highest truth; the farther it separates itself from the lowest, the more it approaches the highest. And this region is proposed as being likened in certain ways to the ethereal heaven, in which the position of the stars and continual motion are found.

For just as that motion itself, by the order of the first mover as cause, is always arranged in heaven, so continual labor is at work in the middle region, so that each intellectual power may perfect its own object and in no way depart from the order naturally implanted in it. Now such powers of the soul are three: memory, understanding, and will.

From these, memory gathers the likenesses and phantasms of things, and extends itself concerning what is arduous. The understanding, by discerning those phantasms, considers them, and here investigates the true. But the will embraces what has been approved by the understanding and ordered, and this is concerned with the known good. When these three powers of the soul rightly preserve their order, they lead the spirit in faith toward heavenly things.

This second region is compared to the ethereal heaven, in which, just as there is continual motion and the position of the stars, so in this middle region there is continual motion and labor against the battles of vices. And just as the motion of the stars fulfills the order of office implanted in it by nature, so each power of the soul, when it is subjected to its own object, is perfected toward the end ordained for it, so far as can happen to wayfarers. But none of these powers can be perfected simply to fullness in this region, since no one in this foreign [unclear] is so perfect that he cannot be more perfect in his own order. For even if memory, in its own object, which is the arduous, could behold the gathered likenesses and phantasms of all creatures, it would not be satisfied unless it could apprehend their principle, which is God; but this is altogether impossible in this region, in which we can form no phantasms or likenesses of God. The understanding also, the counselor, as I might say, of the blind will, extends itself concerning the true; but however much it considers its own object, it is not satisfied until it can apprehend every truth and arrive at the knowledge of the eternal, highest, and infallible truth without the opinion of fantastic speculation. But that perfection is possible for no wayfarer so long as he remains in the body of mortality. The will also, in its own object, which is the good, to be satisfied and true/

will not be able to rejoice, unless it comes to that unchangeable and highest good, which no instability of change overshadows. The highest truth and unchangeable good is God, who said to Moses: “Man shall not see me and live.” And the disciple of the highest truth says: “No one has ever seen God.” But also the prophet, addressing the Lord, says: “Truly, you are a hidden God.” Although, however, the three aforesaid powers of the soul cannot in this life perfectly comprehend their object, nevertheless none should cease from its duty, lest it incur the danger of failing there where it has abandoned the appointed effort. Therefore the citizens of this middle region mortify evil affections in themselves; they adorn themselves with continual virtues; they direct all their works with right intention; they depart not at all from the office of reason.

The citizens of this region are scholastic, speculative, and active men, devoted to various and indeed honorable arts, who subject the sensual or carnal powers to reason; who do not neglect to cleanse these three powers of the soul from all illicit objects; who always raise their intention toward the end of honorable usefulness; who reform the will, in act or in habit, toward its due end. Therefore the coenobite, a lover of this cleansing, who desires to ascend to the third region of the spirit, while remaining in the middle region, must observe the following principal articles.

The summary of the truth of this middle region is expressed in seven principal articles. Whoever desires to make progress in this middle region according to the vow of his profession should diligently take care to observe the following articles; if he neglects to keep them, he shows that he is still a citizen not of the middle but of the lowest region. For, as we said above, no one can remain in this middle region without a continual effort to make progress; in it, not to have progressed is to fail, and not to have ascended is to descend. Therefore the monk who, having overcome the dark region, has at last, with the Lord’s help, deserved to arrive at this middle one should know that he must beware lest he abandon, even for a little, the effort to make progress; but he should always stretch himself toward what lies further, and remember the admonition of the wise man, who says: “Unless you hold yourself constantly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overturned,” that is, your conscience. For it is impossible for anyone to make progress in holy conduct who has neglected daily to renew, through fear of the Lord, the effort to make progress. The effect of this renewal is shown to be ordered when the truth of the articles of the middle region is duly observed. The first article, therefore, is the diligent intention of the coenobite’s end; the second is the due restraint of the sensual powers; the third, the faithful cleansing of the powers; the fourth, the attentive reformation of the works of the lowest region; the fifth, the ordered institution of the true coenobite’s progress; the sixth, the adaptation of the powers for entry into the third region; and the seventh, the exemplary or experiential certainty of all the aforesaid matters.

On the continual and diligent intention of the end of coenobitic conduct. The first article.

Since the end is first in the intention of the wise man, and each thing is judged more perfect in its own kind insofar as it more nearly approaches its end, the monk who cultivates this middle region should always consider why he entered religion; and if he finds his intention ordered, he should strive to continue it; but if he finds it corrupt, he should not neglect to reform it to the rectitude of the due end.

But note that in spiritual exercises the end is described as twofold, through which the virtue of monastic conduct is increased in merits. The first is charity, which is called principal and ultimate, to which all monastic exercises are ordered as to their first cause. Whatever good we do must always and principally be ordered to this end, since no work of virtue receives merit unless charity always establishes the due foundation.

God, says John, is charity; and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him. But everyone who abides in God does not sin. The second end, disposing one toward the first and principal end as though through some suitable means, is called secondary or less principal. The monk must always attend to this end, and through it order his exercises toward the ultimate end. For no one can attain the principal end of charity who neglects to observe the means.

This disposing end toward the ultimate, so far as it pertains to cenobites, according to John Cassian in the Conferences of the Fathers, is to cast away from oneself entirely all cares of the world, to mortify one's own wills, to entrust every disposition and care of oneself to the superior, and to think nothing of tomorrow. For the cenobite who wishes to advance in this middle region must take up the complete denial of himself, and then resign himself wholly into the hands of his superior, so that within, in himself, he may be clean from every dust of self-will, and outwardly, for serving the Lord, free from every secular occupation. Indeed, unless our cenobite has come to this end, he is in no way a true monk, because he still sows corruption in corruptible flesh and by no means observes the virtue of his profession.

This monastic denial of self-will seems chiefly to consist in three things, without which no one is truly to be said to have denied himself. First, the mortification of self-will requires in the monk the eradication of his own judgment, because whoever relies on his own judgment or counsel disdains humbly to be subject to another. For the root from which the defense of self-will arises is called adherence to one's own counsel or judgment. Whoever, established in a monastery, desires to cling to his own judgment, sins gravely against the rule as a usurper of self-will. For it befits the cenobite to live by another's command rather than his own, if toward eternal life through the merit of obedience [unclear]. According to Bernard, [self-will?] is the greatest leprosy of the soul; the more hidden it is, the more pernicious it will be; and the more anyone abounds in it, the sounder he seems to himself to be.

Second, mortification of the will requires the emptying-out of one's own affections, because no one is able to stand rightly ordered amid adversities and advantages, and truly subject to God, who does not strongly restrain his carnal affections. Third, for the mortification of self-will that poverty of spirit is required, lest in things of use, in food, clothing, and the rest, the monk's affections be taken captive; because whoever loves these things too much shows himself, against the rule, to be a lover of self-will. For the true cenobite, a cultivator of this middle region, must fervently devote himself to the doctrine of humility, willingly despise all worldly things for the love of God, and love absolutely nothing except God. If he has anything for use, with the rule permitting it, let him beware of attaching the affection of his heart to it, and let him be ready, at the judgment of the pastor and for the benefit of the brothers, to resign all things with a peaceful heart. Let him always choose the things that are simple and meaner; let him give thanks to God in all things, and, placing his hope and sufficiency in him alone, say cheerfully: In you, Lord Jesus, possessing all things, for your love I willingly despise all things; I shall care nothing at all about transitory things.

Therefore let our devout cenobite always direct the eye of his intention, with faithful consideration, toward this end of the monastic institution; let him never withdraw from the sight of it, because whoever in action forgets the ultimate end wanders like an inexperienced and blind sailor amid the storms of the sea, soon to perish. Let the faithful monk therefore imitate [a sailor?] skilled in [navigation?], so that, just as he, always keeping the harbor before his eyes, strives with attentive solicitude to direct the ship there, so the mind of a good man may always be directed toward God as toward the shore and ultimate end. Archers set up some definite mark for themselves, and, lest their sight be scattered from the fixed target, they close one eye. And just as the arrow of the shooter is directed toward the mark, so the intention of the good monk is always ordered toward God; in it also the eye of lower affection is closed, lest the sharpness of higher consideration be scattered through [unclear]. For it is necessary

to close off the affection of earthly curiosity and the understanding of the wisdom of the flesh, as though by not knowing them, if by the mind’s gaze we desire always to raise ourselves to the due end. And just as the eagle is said to look upon the sun with eyes unstruck by its glare, so the monk, God’s servant, contemplates without interruption the end of the monastic institution. Just as a prudent traveler, as he proceeds with pleasure, considers the lodging toward which he is heading, so a good coenobite, in everything he does, always pants chiefly with fervent desire toward his own end, which is God. But a foolish traveler is one who, when placed on the road, forgets the lodging toward which he is heading, and, straying, knowingly becomes entangled in the various impediments of others. And the monk who does not studiously consider the end of his destination assuredly wanders blind on the road.

Therefore the good monk and lover of his own salvation does not neglect his good endeavor in spiritual exercises, but always raises his affection toward higher things by exercising himself in holy works. A good endeavor is to omit nothing of those things which God has commanded; humbly to obey the shepherd in all things for love of God; always to lift up an affection estranged from earthly things to the memory of heavenly things; and, through continual exercise of spiritual conduct, daily to renew the holy purpose. Whatever good the devout coenobite does, let him always offer it to almighty God with faithful attention; let him despise all earthly things with a strong spirit; let him desire to please God alone.

Let the intention of the coenobitic life always be faithful, so that it wishes to desire nothing other than God’s praise and honor; let its attention be diligent, so that it knows how to summon all the senses of the body and the affections of the soul to God’s service, in order that it may serve its Lord faithfully and seek his glory, not its own.

On the Due Restraint of the Sensual Powers. Article 2.

How useful and how necessary it is for us to restrain the powers of the sensual passions, I think no one is ignorant, especially among monks. Indeed, whoever in this region desires to reach the due end of regular life which we have described must tame his disordered natural habits and movements with prudent constancy, because no one can truly resign himself to another’s command who does not strongly restrain the powers of the sensual passions. For one who desires to make progress must leave behind both the movements and the prudence of the flesh with a steadfast spirit, and show himself a son of divine grace, not of flesh and blood. For Scripture says: If you live according to the command of the flesh, you will die. Indeed, those who sow in the flesh will also reap corruption from the flesh. But flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. But what does the Savior say to us? “A man’s enemies,” he says, “are those of his household.” And who are these household members, if not the sensual powers that oppose the spirit? For concupiscibility and irascibility, our enemies, stir up everything in us against the spirit, and continually disturb the house of conscience with various passions. For so long as these sensual powers carry out their natural movements and courses in a person, they do not permit him to ascend to the freedom of the spirit. Concupiscibility delights in the pleasing things of the sense of the flesh, and the contrary power, irascibility, detests the body’s pains. Meanwhile, as long as this war of the flesh is waged in a person, the monk is considered a restless, carnal cultivator of the lowest region. Therefore whoever desires to come to eternal life must strongly restrain in all things these disordered powers of the senses.

Therefore let the faithful coenobite strive to direct the concupiscible power toward pains that are acceptable to God, and to reform all his affections according to God’s good pleasure. If he has done this, he will confidently pray to the Lord: “My soul has longed to desire your justifications at all times.” And that

will often cry out sweetly with tears: “As the hart longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God.” Then, cleaving to God, prudently to set the irascible power against sensual delights, and diligently to reform it to hatred of vices. Thus the soul, ordered toward its own principle, will not fear to endure any hardships for the love of God, and will begin, by means of the irascible power, bravely to resist all carnal desires. And then the devout cenobite, as his spirit lifts itself up, will cry out: “My soul refused to be comforted.” And that saying of the Apostle: “I counted all things as dung.” For the soul that truly loves God despises everything except him.

From these two powers every disordered affection arises; and good affections likewise are generated from these by opposition. For joy and hope take their beginning from the concupiscible power, and the irascible power brings forth grief and fear. Concerning these Saint Bernard says thus: “The whole heart of man is perverted by four affections; if we bring these back to God, the whole heart of man is converted.”

On the Faithful Cleansing of the Powers.

But we are by no means able to restrain the sensual powers unless we also faithfully cleanse the intellectual powers. For this cleansing great and continual diligence is needed, since the cenobite who is slackened by the torpor of negligence is never cleansed from vicious affections. For he brings back corruption from his errors. Therefore the cenobite, the cultivator of this middle region, must correct his inner powers from every disorder, if he wishes to remain constantly in the pursuit of making progress. These intellectual powers, then, are to be cleansed in this way.

First, indeed, the intellect must be purged of every imagining of vain likenesses, so that, freeing itself from all material things, it may raise itself upward, without any imagining of likeness, to its own principle, and, prudently intent upon its object, may turn itself wholly toward the [ray?] of supreme truth.

Then our faithful cenobite must not neglect to cleanse his memory from every [unclear] and illicit occupation; he must admit no [unclear] base or less useful images for [unclear]; and he must study to repel phantasms of irrational passions and [unclear] meditations, and, so far as can be done, to think nothing foolish.

The will also must be purged from every disordered affection, so that it may will nothing except what right reason [unclear] to be willed, and reject nothing except what reason, according to the judgment of truth, forbids it.

This restriction of the powers and cleansing of the powers is thus spoken of: it grants absolutely nothing to anyone [unclear], except to one who is strong in the struggle by great, discreet, and continual diligence, knowing that the kingdom of God suffers violence, and that no one can subdue the enemy to himself in any way, unless he has resolved to fight against him fiercely and perseveringly. For, as the blessed pontiff Augustine bears witness, we know that a man does not die well unless he has first died to vices and concupiscences. But no one among men truly dies to these except the one who resists his own wills through continual labor, sowing in tears. The mind, therefore, must be armed with saving teachings; strength of patience must be taken up in all things. For just as someone unarmed and impatient of labor cannot throw down an armed enemy, so a monk without spiritual arms and a certain continual force of fighting cannot cleanse his intellectual powers. Although the arms of spiritual warfare are very many in their own usefulness, nevertheless three in particular must be taken up by the monk.

And first, indeed, vigor is necessary for the cenobite in everything that he does, so that he may dare to attack things contrary to the flesh bravely, and may grow lukewarm at no time in his holy purpose. For the exercises of the spirit are hard and utterly contrary to the flesh; in

in which it is not enough to persevere steadfastly; [unclear] scorns to put on the strongest armor. If, therefore, you desire to subject all your affections to the spirit, if you wish to fight successfully against the vices of the flesh, take care to do prudent violence to yourself, and to arm yourself strongly against everything.

Next, a certain holy severity is set before you to be assumed, through which all the contrary and adverse things of this world are borne as almost nothing. For indeed, whoever has once truly assumed this kindly severity of mind for the love of God and with desire for heaven, will thereafter fear no adversities of the flesh so greatly; rather, he is so inwardly flooded with reflection on the divine reward that he seems to take more delight in adversities that occur to him than in prosperities.

But severity is by no means pleasing to the weaker unless it has been tempered somewhat by the sweetness of kindness. Therefore, consequently, this kindness of [soothing?] is to be assumed, so that when, through the weakness of the flesh, someone is tempted in battle, or even wounded, and at times totters, through penance he may soon rise again, to fight more strongly anew. For if the soldier of Christ has fallen in battle, he must, through contrition and the other remedies of penance, rise again as often as necessary, to fight again, until at last, at some time, by God’s mercy, he is able to overcome the adversary. If the just man falls seven times in a day and rises again, how will the sinner, now penitent, not hope for pardon? Rise, therefore, O soldiers, to fight again as often as you have fallen when the adversary prevails; always renew the warfare more strongly from the beginning, so that the enemy whom for the time being you cannot overcome by strength you may at last overcome by perseverance. Do not despair of victory, O faithful cenobite, because you have often been overcome by temptation and have fallen into the snare of vice. Do not lie prostrate any longer because you feel yourself weak, but rise again at once as often as you have fallen, and trust that you have a merciful Lord, by whose help you will at last be victor over the adversary. For no one suddenly becomes supreme, nor is victory over the enemy granted at once to [unclear] soldiers, lest, destined to perish more grievously, they be lifted up in pride.

The possession of a thing acquired with difficulty is always dearer, and a good that is acquired laboriously is guarded with greater diligence. So long does God, the loving Father, permit us, conquered by the temptations of the adversary, to fall at intervals of change into the pit of sin, until, conscious of our weakness, we learn to hope for nothing in our own powers but only in the grace of him alone. But you, man, who often interrupt your purpose by sinning, never delay to rise again; for even if you cannot perfectly subject the enemy to yourself, nevertheless it will be good for you if the last day is able to find you standing and fighting, even after a fall often repeated. But those to whom the mercy of God has granted strength and grace to defeat the adversary, this counsel does not make lax. Nevertheless, let him who stands see that he does not fall.

On the attentive reformation of the works of the first region.

Article IV.

Since indeed, as we taught at the end of the first treatise, this middle region is nearest to the first on its lowest side, in which, if the cenobite has been even a little negligent and slack, he immediately falls back, without any middle state, into the former one. And therefore whoever desires to persist in this region by making progress should always, with attentive vigilance, strive to reform the works of the lowest region. And, lest we be lengthy, whoever desires to practice this reformation in himself should assume in this region works contrary to the eight articles of the first. For, as is prescribed by the tradition of physicians, contraries are cured by contraries.

The citizens of this middle region, therefore, faithful monks, are commanded first to look to this: that they strive to order themselves toward God above all things. This ordering is said to be done well if God, according to the law, is loved above all things from the whole heart. Next, toward his prelate, the devout cenobite

let him show: let him render humble reverence to him; let him strive to love him with sincere charity; and let him keep, according to the rule, all the things that he commands.

The ruler of souls also, having been appointed over the cenobites, should take care to conduct himself and to show himself a true shepherd to the sheep, not a hireling; let him not neglect the salvation of the souls committed to him; let him not put temporal things before spiritual things. Let him hate vices, love the brethren, and show himself exemplary in all good things.

Next, let the brethren cleave to one another as members of one head; let them love one another in the true charity of God, and not withdraw from good zeal. For all of us who, through faith in Christ, trust to come to eternal life by applying ourselves to good works are members of Christ, the supreme head. But whoever persecutes his brother with evil zeal or hatred and other evil affections first separates himself from the head, and then does injury to Christ.

Consequently, let each one show himself ordered with respect to himself: for the love of Christ let him humbly submit himself to all; through humility let him prefer others to himself; and let him believe himself more unworthy than all monks.

In the use of the monastery’s goods let them always beware of exceeding the instruction of the rule; rather, let them strive everywhere to show themselves ordered and faithful in all things. Let them desire to have nothing contrary to the abbot’s will; let them admit no pleasure of the spirit in the use of things.

Then faithful cenobites will take care to order themselves, according to the rule’s instruction, toward contempt of the world, so that they love nothing in this world, but truly despise all things for the love of God.

Let them not neglect to order themselves most diligently to penitence; let them often have recourse to humble confession of their transgressions, since, just as no one is believed to live in this world without sin, so penitence is judged necessary for all, even for monks. Therefore the good cenobite, through the pursuit of compunction, should always learn to have recourse to penitence, humbly to accuse himself of his transgressions in chapter, willingly to perform the imposed penance, and faithfully to amend himself in all things.

On the Ordered Instruction of True Monastic Progress and the Degrees of Humility. Article Five.

The greatest virtue of a monk is humility, and the gravest crime in a cenobite is pride. For a monk who is proud with a swollen mind becomes an imitator and servant of the devil, and is stripped of all virtues, if he had any, since no virtue can subsist in a mind in which pride has happened to dwell. Therefore the cenobite who desires to make progress in this middle region should learn to order himself, through humility, toward the true progress of monastic instruction, because no one truly attains humility except one who dwells upon spiritual pursuits. True progress in regular instruction, excluding all adulterine muses, arises from the degrees of humility, which, through their roots, are set down in the rule as twelve. The roots of this progress come from the pursuit of sacred reading, which gradually leads a person to the fear of the Lord. From reading arises spiritual meditation, from which holy compunction is generated. The more useful mode of cenobitic meditation consists in the memory of the Lord’s passion and in the consideration of God’s benefits. Further, those who, exceeding this middle region, come to tranquility of spirit render their meditations more sublime through contemplation of the divine majesty and excellence. And indeed we shall speak of these in their own place. But these two roots receive growth from the watering of continual prayer, and strengthen into the vigor of a very firm plant. For no meditation makes progress without prayer, and study without it will not save.

From these three roots of spiritual progress arises the fear of the Lord, which is the first degree of humility; from it the other degrees are generated, succeeding in order. But monks who neglect the salutary pursuit of the Scriptures and holy meditations together with continual prayers in no way reach this first degree of humility. But those who [unclear] the first degree

[He] cannot ascend the [first?] step of humility; when will he be able to reach the others? For the second is never ascended if the first is neglected. Therefore he who neglects one ascends none.

The pursuit of sacred reading, however, must not be undertaken for the vanity of the world, nor for the pleasure of a seduced mind, because reading never profits toward compunction when the delight of the flesh or of vanity corrupts it. A monk, moreover, cannot attain devotion through the pursuit of sacred reading unless he strives to change all curiosity into a simple spirit. Therefore whoever desires to advance from the reading of the Scriptures toward compunction, whoever [desires] to ascend to humility, must choose [unclear], but only that which can more fully stir the mind to the love of God. For this purpose the reading of [unclear] seems to me sufficiently suitable, because by memory it is often recalled to love of him. We also willingly admit miracles and the repeated torments of punishments or joys of separated souls, in conformity with the Catholic faith, by which we have found that sluggish hearts are often stirred to compunction. Finally, the passions of the holy martyrs greatly kindle the fervor of devotion; in them, while we bring back to mind the unconquerable charity of Christ, moved to compunction by the example of such great constancy, touched as though by a certain fire of love, we sigh over our imperfection. From reading the material of meditation is taken, and as the former has been, so the latter will be. Not the shameful songs of poets, not the curious doctrines of philosophers, not the swelling writings of rhetoricians: these rather choke the fervor that must be kindled. If, therefore, you wish to persist in good meditations, do not occupy your mind with readings other than holy and devoutly known ones. For indeed not even one [unclear] is generated from study. Let him who studies for the knowledge of this world read those things that suit him for erudition; but let him who seeks compunction think upon those things that kindle the soul to the love of God through fear.

Frequent reading, therefore, should take its beginning from the last things that await us; then let the deeds of the holy fathers be read, so that the memory of future things may shake the mind to the fear of God, and the exemplary life of the saints may kindle the desire of imitation. For the wise man says: Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever. The life of the holy fathers is set before us as an example, and the destruction of the wicked is recounted to us for our instruction, so that virtue rewarded may move desire, and iniquity punished may forbid the license of sinning. Therefore the devout cenobite should always recall to memory the examples and virtues of the saints; he should consider the brief pleasure of the wicked, but their eternal torment, so that by fearing unhappiness he may deserve to escape it, and by insisting on their virtues obtain their perpetual joy. The distinct condition of the good and the wicked is no light matter, since each is described as destined to remain forever and is bounded by no end. O eternity, always to be feared by all mortals, in which after this life there is no fear of consummation for the righteous, and no hope of deliverance for the perverse. Let him who can consider what eternity is; let him who dares imagine an end, and when in eternity he has found nothing other than eternity, let him understand how nothing is all the time in which he lives in this world. For indeed, once the spirit has been stripped of the flesh, it is necessarily compelled to enter the abyss of eternity; and the condition that it has once obtained according to its merits [unclear] without end. Whoever shall have departed once from this life without the recompilation [unclear] of penitence will remain to be tormented without end with the demons in hell. From these meditations fear [enters] the mind, and little by little one comes to love. But so that we may be able to lead the cenobite successively through these roots to charity, it pleases us to explain briefly, in order, the steps of humility described in the Rule.

The first degree of humility, therefore, is described by Saint Benedict in the Rule as the fear of God, which is called the beginning of wisdom. The fear of the Lord is handed down under a threefold distinction: namely servile, initial, and filial, which is also called chaste. From this threefold distinction three roots are said to proceed, according to which the beginning cenobite ought to order his meditations. For each root has its own proper meditations, and when one is rightly disposed, another, better one is always generated.

For from servile fear, taken up not merely in a servile manner but prudently and virtuously, there proceed meditations on horror and punishments, which, restraining the soul from sin, gradually introduce filial fear. For indeed, when by consideration of punishments the mind is turned to horror, the boldness of sinning is restrained, because the servant who fears blows keeps the commandments of the Lord. But this servile fear alone is not sufficient for meriting the fatherly inheritance; nevertheless, as an initial effect, it disposes one toward filial fear, which is sufficient.

For initial fear is placed midway between the two, and is easily changed from servile into filial. This initial fear receives meditations concerning the last things, and fears both to incur punishments and to lose the sweet homeland. And here [unclear] is placed in the Rule, where its roots are also described.

Filial fear, however, embraces its meditations in love, since it fears nothing else except that the beloved father should be offended. Of this fear the wise man says: The fear of the Lord is glory and boasting, joy and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart and will give joy and gladness unto length of days. And again: It will be well with him who fears God at the last, and on the day of his death he will be blessed. This fear is also called chaste, because it detests evils not from fear of punishments but from love alone.

From this threefold fear we see three breadths of spiritual exercises arising around the degrees of humility, and individual exercises corresponding to individual fears. For servile fear performs its exercises in one way, initial fear applies itself to virtues in another way, and filial fear proceeds in its works in a much different way. For just as the affections of hearts arise in various ways, so the exercises of one fear are done in different ways. In one way the publican, mindful of his crimes, feared the sentence of the judge; in another way Jerome said that he heard the voice of the trumpet calling the dead to judgment. For the holy Gospel says of the former: Standing afar off, the publican would not lift up his eyes to heaven, but striking his breast he said, God, be merciful to me, a sinner. But that blessed Jerome says: Whether I drink or eat, I always think I hear that trumpet sounding in my ears: Rise, dead, come to judgment. The compunction of each arises from fear, but both are not generated from the desire of one affection. For the publican, terrified by the guilt of his sins, feared the sentence of the just judge, and therefore, being compunct, he said: God, be merciful to me, a sinner. Jerome, however, is not shaken by fear from the guilt of [unclear], but, founded in charity and reckoning himself a useless servant, reveres the abyss of divine justice.

The second degree is to relinquish one’s own will for the love of God, and in no respect to love one’s own willing against the Rule.

This degree arises from the first ascent of humility and is raised into the third. For indeed, he who fears God, and truly fears to be separated from him and to undergo punishments, hates nothing more than his own will. For the faithful cenobite knows that every sin arises from one’s own will alone, and therefore he detests it as the gate of hell. For that blessed man truly said: Take away one’s own will, and now there will be no hell. For nothing burns in hell except one’s own will; nothing loses the grace of God except voluntary fault. Therefore whoever, truly fearing God, fears to lose his grace, greatly fears his own will as the betrayer of his soul. Consideration of the danger of one’s own will makes the cenobite despise his own willing and deny himself to himself. And this denial of one’s own will and of oneself is accomplished in three ways, as will be said in what follows.

And first, indeed, he denies himself to himself who strives to live according to the teaching of eternal Wisdom and not according to his own impulses, and to obey Christ in all things when he counsels him to humility. Therefore let the Savior say to the cenobite: If you wish to deny yourself to yourself and follow me, turn away your eyes, lest they see harmful things; your ears, lest they hear vain things; and in place of the sweet things of this world take bitter things. Learn to despise the pleasures of your body, to love tranquillity and peace of heart, to receive all tribulations for love of me patiently and joyfully, and desire to be seen by all as base and contemptible. Consequently learn to break your own wills in all things, to mortify the desires of the flesh, to despise all earthly things, and, as far as can be done, to conform your life with all your strength to the way of life of your Savior. For he who says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked. Whoever has done these things has well denied himself.

Second, the denial of one’s own will is then rightly perfected when the advantages of others are put before one’s own. For the holy apostle says: Not seeking the things that are their own, but the things that are others’. For according to the judgment of Bernard, the soul is laid down for the brethren as often as their advantages are preferred to one’s own interests for the love of God.

Third, the resignation of one’s own will receives the fullness of perfection when the cenobite, contrite and wholly bound over to God, desires out of love to serve him freely, without regard for reward. And this most holy resignation of one’s own will makes a man very near to God and always rests in his love.

Just as this resignation of oneself takes its foundation from the second degree of humility, so also it necessarily requires an inward resignation, in every way, to the will of God in all things. For the Lord says in the Gospel: I have not come to do my own will, but that of the Father who sent me. Perfect resignation, therefore, is that by which the human will is wholly subjected to the divine will and conformed to it out of entire love. For thus the Lord himself taught us to pray: Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth. And that saying of the psalm-writer: Into thy hands I commend my spirit. Never in this world is one lived more securely than if the human will is perfectly subjected to God.

Indeed, the perfect resignation of oneself, by which the cenobite truly subjects his will to God, shows the straight way to the highest good without any intermediary. Here there is the greatest tranquillity of mind, the utmost security is in the heart, because the soul that strives to subject itself perfectly to God will no longer be able to fear any contrary thing of this world except sin alone. Whatever adversity should rush upon it, with the Lord’s help it has learned to overcome; whatever advantage it desires, it understands that it possesses in the Lord alone. It despises all adverse things for love of him; it has placed all good things in his love. For that devout man spoke prudently: Let go of all things, and you will find all things. Leave behind covetousness, and you will find true peace.

Finally, in order that this resignation of one’s own will may receive the fullness of consummation, it implores, so to speak, the support of a threefold aid.

The first is placed in the virtue of perseverance, so that a will once denied is never taken back. For that holy Bernard says to the contemners of this aid: Why do you again meddle with yourselves, you who once, by mature deliberation, handed over your will to us? For the monk who has once handed over his will to God into the hands of the abbot does not take it back without the crime of sacrilege.

The second thing required for perfect resignation of the will is that it never be relaxed. Hence the Lord says to the lukewarm soul in the Apocalypse: I have a few things against you, because you have left your first charity, that is, your fervor.

Third, resignation of the will is perfected if it is never broken off. For the Savior says: He who has persevered unto the end shall be saved. Therefore when you see a cenobite inquire

whether moved by anger. You should know that the whole mass of the temptation proceeds from lack of resignation; and you will never cure this sickness’s disease unless you first persuade him to the resignation of a renounced will.

The third degree of humility is to subject oneself in all obedience to one’s superior for the love of God, and to show oneself an imitator of Christ by works, not by words only; concerning him the holy Apostle says: “He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” This degree takes its beginning from the second and raises its ascent as far as the third. For just as the second mortifies one’s own will by denying it, so this one, through humble subjection, lays the foundation of holy work. The former subjects itself wholly to the divine will; the latter, for the love of God, also obeys men.

The keeping of one degree without the observance of the other does not suffice in a monk; nor is the will of a cenobite subjected to the divine ordering if it disdains to obey the command of a superior.

Therefore the true cenobite places all his joy in the virtue of holy obedience; he considers it the greatest gain to fulfill in all things the will of his shepherd; he believes it a grave loss to the soul if he should find that he has committed even a little outside obedience. For he always considers with faithful devotion what the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me.” Hence that blessed Bernard says to the monks: “Whatever a man commands in God’s stead must be received no otherwise than if God himself commanded it in person.” Therefore the true monk should prefer this subjection of obedience to every sacrifice, should do absolutely nothing against its integrity, and should continually say to himself what is written: “Obedience is better.” The rule says: therefore all things are to be done with the abbot’s will.

But this degree, as we have said, arises from the second, because he who, through fear of God, perfectly abandons his own will now seeks nothing else in this world than to follow that will in all things. But because God speaks once and does not repeat the same thing, weak man cannot know the will of the Most High; therefore he has committed himself [unclear] into the hands of his prelate. Let the cenobite therefore obey the vicar of Christ according to the Rule, and without doubt he will fulfill the will of God.

This obedience, however, is owed strictly to prelates according to the Gospel and the monastic rule; for although mutual obedience among the brothers is good, still it must never be preferred to the command of a superior. They command monks to render discreet obedience to one another, and, with the precepts of superiors preserved, to anticipate one another in mutual services. And, to bring an example from our custom: everyone must be obeyed according to order. If a brother calls upon you, obey willingly; if a senior commands something else, set aside the command of the first and obey him. Again, if the prior of the convent interposes his command, all mutual obedience of the brothers will cease. But if the abbot’s command intervenes, no obedience to any other will have force to the contrary. For he is believed to act first in the monastery in Christ’s stead, and therefore he is preferred to all.

There are seven gradual circumstances of the virtue of holy obedience, which blessed Bernard described thus. The first degree of obedience is to obey willingly, namely that you have no will of your own at all, but believe your shepherd’s good pleasure to be entirely your own. The second is to obey simply, so that you do neither more nor otherwise than what has been commanded you, nor, by doing less, omit anything. The third is to obey cheerfully, so that you display serenity in your face and show sweetness in your voice. The fourth is to obey swiftly, so that the hand is not slower in the work than the command is in the voice. The fifth is to obey manfully, lest one withdraw his strength from the command, and pretend that he is weak and unequal to the precepts. The sixth is to obey humbly, not proudly, not arrogantly, not contentiously; since unless obedience is humble, it will bring back not reward but punishment. The seventh is to obey perseveringly, because obedience that is interrupted before completion is not true obedience; and only he who perseveres unto the end is rewarded.

The fruit of obedience, however, is everlasting, and is bounded by no end whatsoever. Almighty God obeys our prayers only so far as we obey our superiors. Do not flatter yourself, stiff-necked monk, about persistence in prayer, for he who despises Christ’s vicar in the monastery: Christ does not hear him when he prays. Humility raises up prayer; obedience commends it. For obedience, as one of the fathers said, is the salvation of all the faithful, the mother of all virtues, the finder of the kingdom of heaven. Obedience opens the heavens, closes the gates of hell, becomes a companion-dweller with the angels, and is regarded as the food of all the saints. But the monk who casts off subjection to obedience runs toward death.

The fourth degree of humility is patience in adversities, concerning which our holy father Benedict speaks in the Rule: if a monk, under obedience, embraces patience with a silent conscience amid hard and adverse things, or even amid any injuries inflicted on him. This degree too takes its beginning from the third, for no one is truly to be called obedient if he has been found impatient. For, as that divine Chrysostom says, he cannot be acceptable to the king who has been subject to the enemy; nor is he truly subject to Christ who has been enslaved to passionate and impatient flesh. For no one will be able to conquer a fierce enemy unless he has first learned to fight bravely against him. Patience is very necessary for us, for no virtue is lawfully perfected if patience is lacking.

Indeed, with blessed Gregory bearing witness, it is of greater merit to receive adversities patiently for God than to toil in good works. And Saint Jerome says: He who believes that tribulation has come upon him for his sins calls forth God’s mercy toward himself more fully for doing good. Therefore let the cenobite learn to set the virtue of patience against all things that happen to him, if he desires to triumph over his enemies. For he who suffers conquers; he who murmurs is overcome.

Moreover, in three things the virtue of patience is especially necessary, and is rewarded with the highest prizes. In insults of words, the patience of a prudent man and lover of God preserves the purpose of humility; in the removal of goods and temporal advantages it receives increase; and in injury to the body, with silent conscience, it strengthens the practice of virtue. Now consider, O faithful soul, how your most loving Savior Jesus endured these three things most patiently for your redemption; and if you believe that you love him, do not be troubled to bear similar things with patience for love of him.

From the three degrees immediately preceding we constitute one end of the cenobites, which, as it seems to us, we reasonably call threefold in degree. For by three degrees, namely the second, third, and fourth, the end of the cenobitic institution is perfected, and the renunciation of one’s own will is consummated. For where patience, the preserver of the virtues, is joined to the renunciation of one’s own will and to obedience, every pleasure and concern of the body is mortified. Whoever has deserved to ascend this threefold degree has fulfilled the Lord’s commandment, in which he says in the Gospel: He who wishes to come after me, let him deny himself through the second degree of humility, and take up his cross through the third, and follow me through the fourth.

The fifth degree of humility is true confession of sins, into which the faithful cenobite is said to ascend if he confesses to his abbot, with humble trust, all evil thoughts coming into his heart, or any evils committed in secret. For indeed, if anything is committed amiss through impatience at the adversary’s suggestion in the preceding threefold degree, in this one it is restored through contrition and humble confession. For no one is found so perfect that he does not contract the stain of earthly conduct, as Scripture says: In many things we all offend. For no one is clean from sin, not even an infant whose life is one day upon the earth. Necessarily, therefore, this degree follows the fourth without any intervening step, and in it all the negligences of the preceding degrees are amended. True confession lifts up the soldier who falls in battle, heals him when wounded by the enemy, and comforts him when weak and fainthearted. Whoever, therefore, [unclear] to stand in battle and conquer

... the enemy bravely: let him more often have recourse to the protections of true confession. For it is impossible for one wounded by the enemy to recover health if he neglects to open the wound itself to the physician. Therefore you, faithful cenobite, who desire to save your soul and to be a good soldier of Jesus Christ, do not omit humble confession, because you will never be able to conquer the devil better than if you take care faithfully to disclose to your abbot all the thoughts he suggests to you and your sins. It is certain to me, and proved by the destruction of many, that the cenobite who refuses to keep this degree commits himself to being overcome by many temptations of the enemy.

The sixth degree of humility arises from true confession: that the monk should consider himself vile for all things and unworthy. For according to the Rule we believe him to be a true monk whom we see, from humble patience, to be content with every vileness and extremity in food and clothing. But that vileness is placed in customary inconveniences. For the former willingly embraces patience in cheaper garments, foods, and whatever necessities of the body; the latter delights in serving the sick, lepers, and the cast off, in being confounded, degraded, and despised in all things. Therefore the monk who is truly dead to the flesh and the world should be content with every vileness and extremity; he should show himself a faithful worker in all things, and yet, because of the corruption of nature by which he offends in many things, he should believe himself vile and unworthy. For truly whatever good is done in this world, however holily and religiously one lives in this age, it can suffice no one for meriting eternal life unless God’s great mercy deigns to come to his aid. We receive the greatest things for the least; we expect the kingdom of God not as owed to us from our own merit, but from the grace of the promises. For the holy Apostle says: The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us. For if we receive the justice of God without mercy, we are worthy of hell. We all incur wrath by sinning, but we obtain love from grace. No one is saved except through grace; no one is damned except through justice. Meanwhile, however, in order that we may obtain the grace of God, the zeal of our good will is required; without that grace nothing in us works toward merit. For although no one does good by his own holy powers, nevertheless no one does a good thing well unwillingly. For the grace of God and freedom of choice stand in such relation to one another that one without the other cannot suffice for saving a human being, but both must necessarily come together for the operation of virtue. Since therefore without the grace of God we can do nothing good, we ought to esteem ourselves vile and unworthy for all things, so that, while we submit ourselves to God in humility, we may always obtain greater things. And therefore this sixth degree is the merit of confession and the single foundation of all the preceding degrees. For as long as the cenobite remains in this degree of humility, he will stand firm in the former ones.

The seventh degree of humility is not only to believe oneself from the inmost affection of the heart to be viler than all, but also to desire with a simple mind that others believe and say this about him. This condition of holy humility is placed on high, and in this time is loved by few monks. For the first condition of this profound humility seems to consist in this: that the monk ought from the heart to esteem himself viler than all. The second is that he should rejoice to be esteemed vile and abject by all, and should desire this from the inmost affection of the heart without pretense. The third condition is placed in a higher dwelling: namely, that from the same affection the monk should delight in being treated most vilely and trampled upon by all. Rooted in this humility, the cenobite loves reproach and insult; he does not fear to be despised and most vilely cast aside, because, submitting his whole self in the love of God, he humbly places himself, and hastens toward insults as toward feasts with the greatest cheerfulness. But so that you may understand the truth of this seventh degree, read the following considerations.

The first consideration directs the mind to hope in divine love, which arises from a certain pious confidence. For although a human being does not know whether he is worthy of love, nevertheless each person can in some measure recognize it from the disposition of his own heart:

what he ought to think about his own state, good or bad.

Second, one must consider that this good disposition of the heart, and of the will ordered toward God, is a sign of the love of God and of the approval of good works. For thus, when the Lord was born in the flesh, the angels sang: Peace on earth to men of good will.

Third, it should be noted that, just as a good disposition of the heart always orders and prompts the mind through holy exercises toward the fear of God and the practice of the virtues, so the negligence of an evil disposition especially inclines it toward vices and acedia. Consideration of this difference gives rise to conjecture.

Fourth, one must consider that an evil disposition of the heart hinders and makes void the grace of God and merits in a person, since it makes the soul vile, ignoble, and degenerate, and always disposes it toward graver and worst things. Indeed, the root of evils of tongue and deed comes from an evil heart, as is clear in Saul and in many similar cases.

The fifth consideration is that evil in deed and tongue is never well examined unless the evil of the heart is first truly known. But each person can examine his own heart better than another can, and consider what sort of person lies hidden within himself. Therefore for the cenobite to whom care of another has not been entrusted, it is enough to inspect his own heart diligently, and in no way to occupy himself with scrutiny of another’s heart. But the shepherd of monks, to whom care of souls is entrusted, is also commanded to know the face of his flock.

Sixth, it should be noted from these things that it is very rash to wish to examine another’s heart and to judge the inward parts of brothers from words and deeds. The Lord knows who are his; nor is it granted to a man, without reason of office, to become a rash judge of another’s heart.

Seventh, it should be noted that a small evil of one’s own heart does more harm to the one who knows it in himself than a great evil suspected doubtfully concerning another’s heart. For the former is to be lamented, because it is certain and known; the latter is to be piously excused, because it is unknown.

Eighth, one must consider that since each person sees many imperfections in his own heart which he cannot recognize in others, on account of these he ought to judge himself inferior, insofar as they are obstacles to grace. But insofar as they defile the soul, he should despise himself as [more vile than all others?], even if he knows their public crimes. For since the root of their heart is utterly unknown to him, he cannot know with certainty how divine election has been ordained from eternity concerning him. Who would have believed that the thief crucified with the Lord was chosen from eternity, [if] he judged him according to works? All things turn to good for the elect, since where sin is seen to have abounded, often, by the will of divine election, greater grace is found. For divine love regards and embraces its elect from eternity, and looks upon them, as elect, not according to the misery in which they now are, but according to future glory. Therefore the cenobite is careful not to detract from others; he is careful not to judge others, if he desires to escape eternal death. For who are you, that you judge another’s servant? He stands to be judged by his own lord alone.

But the disposition of this seventh degree, because of that clause, “from the inmost disposition of the heart,” has a threefold root of its origin, namely truth, hope, and charity. For indeed, when the faithful cenobite sees that he does not have his being from himself, he truly thinks himself, insofar as he is from himself, to be nothing; and consequently, in the same respect, he considers his works, insofar as they come from himself who is nothing, to be nothing, since he is not unaware that nothing is made from nothing. Therefore the monk [rejoices with?] truth, who in this respect judges himself and his works to be nothing, because he fears incurring the vice of falsehood if he were to believe himself to be something great. And therefore, withdrawing from himself, he abandons himself, and places his being, living, and ability in God alone.
