Second, this disposition arises from hope of acquiring greater grace, because when a person, through humility, abandons himself, he approaches nearer to the grace of God. Third, the humility of this disposition takes its beginning from love of God, and continually receives increase in it. For whoever perfectly loves God seeks nothing other than his honor in all things, nor does he know how to exalt himself in anything, and for God’s sake he desires to be subject to all. But the more [unclear] reproaches and injuries

he is cast down; rejoicing all the more, he is glad in the Lord. He sees himself to be wretched, so that in himself he may proclaim the Lord glorious. He who truly loves his Lord seeks nothing other than his glory.

It is clear from what has been said that the perfect charity which is promised to those ascending the steps of humility is shown in this seventh step. For the other five steps that follow in the Rule add nothing to the perfection of the inner man who is established in the seventh, but rather order the outer man, lest he disturb the inner. Finally, from this seventh step we can erect certain new ascents of humility, and in them raise all the other steps higher. For filial fear resides more fervently in him who, by the breadth of love, can make greater progress.

Now that the ascents of the heart up to the step of charity have been learned, let the cenobite consider with what zeal, with what effort, with what perseverance he ought to exercise himself in these things, so that he may reach this seventh step of love. But he who does not always strive to advance in these steps of humility should know that he sins against the Rule; and unless by a holier effort he comes to his senses in repentance, he incurs the sentence of damnation. For thus the Rule says: “But if at any time he has acted otherwise, let him know that he is to be condemned by him whom he mocks.” But if anyone making too little progress in religion is deemed guilty by divine judgment, what else does one who abandons the effort of advancing deserve than to receive the sentence of damnation? For where, according to the Rule, one is held guilty for lesser progress even among those who are striving to advance, monks who despise every effort of advancing are without doubt condemned by the sentence of the Judge. Therefore, if you do not wish to incur the danger of damnation, strive continually to preserve the effort of advancing under the Rule.

Since we have said that the other five steps of humility pertain to the custody of the inner man, let us also expound them briefly. For the monk who neglects to order his outward conduct according to the Rule will not remain ordered for long in inward things. For just as a body stripped of clothing is corrupted, so humility without conduct is [unclear].

The eighth step of humility, then, is set down in the Rule thus: if a monk does nothing except what the common rule of the cenobium, or the examples of the elders, encourage. In this step, singularity of outward conduct contrary to the Rule is forbidden to monks; but inward singularity of greater charity and humility is forbidden to no one. Therefore let no one prefer his own inventions to the holy Rule; let no one place his own customs before the examples of the elders, because to stand in the seventh step is not enough for one who does not keep the rule of the community.

The ninth step of humility follows from the Rule, through which excessive talkativeness is forbidden. For it befits a monk to keep silence, especially while he sits in the midst of his seniors. Indeed, he who speaks without being questioned is deservedly regarded as a fool.

The tenth step of humility forbids readiness of laughter and levity, because whoever takes delight in laughter is shown to be foolish and estranged from the fear of God.

The eleventh step of humility enjoins modesty and maturity upon the monk, so that when the opportunity and permission to speak are granted, he may speak with humble gravity, without laughter and anger. Let the monk’s speech be rare, brief, and reasonable, because it does not befit one who wishes to please the Most High to say useless things.

The twelfth step of humility teaches the monk to order the outer man, in appearance and bearing, from a humble heart, and to demonstrate also by outward conduct how devout he is inwardly. And although this step is last in the order of all, nevertheless in the practice of those beginning to advance it is first. And therefore Bernard, in describing these twelve steps of humility, begins from this one, and by ascending to the first, as I might put it, descends through the order. For no one easily advances inwardly to compunction of heart and fear of God who does not order his conduct outwardly.

On the devout fitting of the powers for entrance into the third region. Article VI.

When, by the degrees of humility, the innermost powers of a person have especially been purified, founded, and reformed, it is now said to be very necessary in monks that they be fitted more devoutly for entrance into the third region. This diligence in striving toward higher things is, as we have said, necessary for the cenobite, because wherever the effort to advance is laid aside, acquired virtue is utterly dissipated. No one is permitted to stand still in this second region; rather, we are all commanded to ascend to the third through continual effort. For truly this continual movement casts all the slothful and lukewarm back into the first region of the flesh, but gently and without violence always impels the humble and those fervent in desire toward the third. Therefore whoever has deserved to obtain from the Lord, through humility, the reformation of his powers is already near to the third region of the spirit. In order that he may be able to enter it powerfully, it is necessary that, by most diligently fitting the powers of his soul, he order them to their several operations. The intellect is then said to be rightly fitted for entrance into the third region when it is illuminated to know the highest truth according to its capacity.

For the same purpose the memory is ordered when it is fully absorbed in retaining and cherishing the highest truth. But if the will is disposed to loving the Highest, which is God, it is well fitted for the entrance of the spirit.

Now, in order that the cenobite may be able to attain the purification of the intellectual powers, it is necessary that, dying to the world, the mind, pacified from every inward and outward tumult, should rest, so that, buried within the bosom of divine love, it may remain there and never withdraw from the sweetness of inward union. To this rest of the mind [unclear]. The first degree of good will lays the beginnings of the virtues, which is called right will.

For the soul which, consenting to the law of God, is subjected to God through right will, even if it still seems weak, is directed to the path of virtue. For virtue is perfected while the flesh resists, and how right the will is is proved by the force of the spirit. Yet often a will is called right and good even when it is found to be less strong. The good that it loves it cannot always accomplish; the evil that it hates it grieves that it has committed through weakness. Through the weakness of the flesh it is very close to the lowest region, but through rightness of intention and the effort to advance it is continually kindled toward the liberty of the spirit. For the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind that thinks many things. O who could describe this battle between spirit and flesh, where the spirit itself desires to subject the flesh to itself through right will, and the weak flesh always resists the spirit through contrary desires?

The second degree is a will strong in rectitude, so that it both bravely flees the evil that it hates against the impulses of the flesh, and strongly grasps by action the good that it loves, although with labor.

The third degree is a devout will, by which the mind, with enlarged heart, embraces the way of God’s commandments and delights in them as in all riches. For truly the will does not long remain strong if it has not been devout in the commandments of God.

The fourth degree is a full will, so that a man does not divide his powers at all, but continually stretches himself wholly toward his God through the denial of all things. Three things are necessary for this degree, so that good will may be made full in us.

The first is complete denial of oneself, because the will is shown still to be weak if it is not mortified through every kind of self-denial.

The second thing required for a full good will is perfect resignation [unclear]; if anyone desires to apprehend it, let him fervently ascend the third degree of humility. F ii

The third member necessary for the fourth degree of good will is called the total extension of the will toward God; through it the soul, admitted into divine love and sweetly burning, is in a certain way transformed into that same love, and is often admitted into the third region.

Finally, this transformation into divine love, according to Bernard's opinion, is love, loving affection, adherence, conjunction, charity, or fruition; no one can attain it unless he has learned to mortify all the affections of his lower spirit. For the spirit of a man who has his heart raised upward into God is called perfect will, and is united with God by a most sweet bond. In these degrees of good will, therefore, the faithful cenobite must direct his effort upward without interruption, and always examine with prudent zeal how much he is advancing or falling short. For Saint Bernard says here: Just as he who remains in a vicious will is condemned, so he is blameworthy who does not strive to advance in other things. For where the effort to advance is laid aside, the danger of falling back is incurred.

Concerning the exemplary and experiential [aspect] of all the aforesaid. Article VII.

Although a man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, nevertheless each person, by diligently examining his conscience, can recognize what he ought to think about the condition of his state. What sort each person is inwardly, hidden within himself, the testimony of his own conscience makes manifest. Therefore, so that the cenobite may clearly discern the condition of his state, he must observe three things in his conscience, according to John Castellensis on the Rule; without these no one becomes a good Christian, no one is judged a good man or monk.

The first thing, therefore, required for a good man is the testimony of a good conscience, namely that no mortal sin lie hidden in the conscience. For the mind that is polluted by the guilt of mortal sin testifies that the state of the conscience is evil.

Therefore each monk must diligently examine himself and carefully cleanse himself of the faults he has committed, according to the ordinance of the Church. But he who, on examining his conscience, finds it clean from mortal sin should offer humble praises to God and not neglect to add the examination of the following things.

The second thing necessary for a good man, accordingly, is to intend God principally in all works, and to order all things, as far as he can, to his praise and honor. But if, because the multitude and variety of works impede him, a man cannot always actually have God before his eyes, let him at least habitually conform his intention of living according to the most pleasing will of God to this desire.

The third is that in all things he obey God and holy mother Church and the prelates set over him, and not depart from the path of right and enlightened reason; for whoever despises this threefold obedience has denied the faith. It is necessary, therefore, to show equal obedience to these three in right order, according to the ordinance of reason, so that the life of the monk may remain, without fear, irreproachable in its actions.

These three things, possessed with humble sincerity, make a good man and show the state of a conscience that hopes well in the Lord. But a man to whom one of these is lacking is not perfectly good, even if he seems to be good. But if one who repents of his sins has resolved henceforth to fulfill these three things, he is now made good and pleasing to God, however evil he had been before. Moreover, so that from a good man a good religious or spiritual man may be born, three other things are required, according to the aforesaid Castellensis.

The first thing required for making a good religious is that purity of heart be cleansed, through zeal for discipline, from every emulation or incitement of the flesh. This purity is never better acquired than if the world, with all things, is despised.

The second thing through which a good man is made a good religious is called spiritual freedom in God. This, of things

with all phantasms excluded, it can raise itself, free in all its exercises, upward to God, and in thanksgiving with devout prayers lift itself continually without impediment.

In the third way a good man is made spiritually good: when, through the desire of love, the spirit is united with God [unclear]. These two last things make our cenobite spiritual, and often introduce him to the citizens of the third region. Whoever, therefore, wishes rightly to trust in the testimony of his own conscience should strive humbly to exercise himself in the aforesaid things, because one never prudently presumes upon safety when danger is not avoided. And what is so dangerous as always to live in negligence and sins, and to refuse to amend the errors one has committed? The confidence of the just, arising from the testimony of a good conscience, is always best, and is continually subject to God in humble service. But the impious and sinners, disturbed by their own actions, raise themselves against God, and do not trust in the testimony of conscience, but rather presume vainly.

There follow the seven roots of divine fear, which are laid fundamentally in the first degree of humility.

Since this second region chiefly instructs the cenobite through the degrees of humility proceeding from the fear of God in the aforesaid order, it is necessary for him to recognize clearly the roots of that fear, if he wishes to arrive, by ascending, at the love of God. Therefore, so that we may be able to construct this spiritual house to perfection, we must place those roots in order in the foundation. We did not, however, set them out in the first degree of humility, lest by excessive prolixity we should confuse the order of the things to be said. There are, then, seven roots of the fear of God, through which the cenobite is brought to compunction and, by advancing in true humility, is more strongly rooted.

The first root of the fear and love of God is the intent meditation upon the incomprehensible divine majesty, which is understood so much the less, the more curiously it is investigated by man. For the prophet says: Truly thou art a hidden God. This meditation generates wonder at divine perfection; wonder causes reverence; from reverence arises fear of majesty; and from fear worship is produced. But meditation on the highest goodness is divided, according to the present purpose, into seven conditions, which are not unsuitably fitted to the seven days of the week, or even to the seven canonical hours. And although that highest and most perfect goodness abundantly suffices for us as matter for meditation, nevertheless, because it belongs to few to be able to rise to invisible things without visible things, we wish to raise the minds of the weak through things known to things unknown. For the holy Apostle says: The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are beheld, being understood through the things that have been made; his everlasting power also and divinity, so that they are without excuse.

First, therefore, the wondrous power of God’s might is praiseworthy in the principal work of creation: for he who was able to bring forth all things out of nothing created, by his will alone, things so great, so solid, so varied, and so noble. From this consideration arises wonder at divine power, through which man is stirred to the fear of God.

Second, the provident wisdom of God is praiseworthy, because, knowing all things, he orders them, and governs by his providence all things that he has created. He knows all things, understands all things; by his counsel he disposes all things; by his command he encloses all things. For, as a certain lover of worldly wisdom said, God is a sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. He is within all things and is not enclosed; he is outside all things and is not shut out; he is beneath all things and is not oppressed; he is above all things and is not borne up. He includes all things, for although he is wholly everywhere, he is confined in no place; great and immense, he is bounded by no quantity. He himself orders all things as he wills; stable in himself and always immovable, he changes the vicissitudes of things; he mercifully prepares eternal rewards for the good without passion of mind; angered without disturbance, he condemns the unjust. Great without magnitude, immense without quantity, he has set a limit to things; governing the world, he disposes all things.

Third, the merciful clemency of God is praiseworthy in our redemption

is: for the man whom he created in his own image, fallen so wretchedly into the pit of damnation, he restored so mercifully. O what shall I, a little worm, indeed nothing in comparison with my maker, render to the supreme and incomprehensible majesty, who, when I did not exist, created me by his power, and, when I had perished, became man for me and, dying on the cross, redeemed me? What shall I repay to you, mediator of God and men, Jesus, savior of the world, who, though you are God exalted and inestimable, became man for me, the vilest, and were willing to undergo things so vile and unworthy? Behold, my heart speaks to you; all my inward parts bow toward you, because no voice can express what, concerning your most innocent passion, you grant your faithful inwardly to feel in their hearts.

Fourth, in the work of our justification, the kindly patience of God is worthy of praise, because he not only mercifully bears with sinners, but also calls those who are to be justified to repentance by the promises of eternal joys. Who could suffice to praise this clemency of the most indulgent father, who so mercifully justifies sinners returning to him, gives after a fall the grace of meriting, ordains manifold occasions for living well, and supplies his sacraments to the penitent as certain vessels of grace? Finally, for compunction, instruction, consolation, and thanksgiving, he pours the Holy Spirit himself into his faithful, making friends and sons out of enemies. He does not consider what sort of sinner a man was before; he seeks only that thereafter he remain faithful to him. Great is the clemency of divine compassion, which so mercifully receives the penitent to pardon, and even promises them great rewards after guilt.

Fifth, the deep justice of God is worthy of praise in the damnation of the reprobate, because he permits no evil to pass unpunished, depriving the sinner of the good which, by sinning, the fool does not fear to lose. Finally, to speak in our fashion, the supreme purity of God is shown worthy of praise in this, that it abominates every sin and vice as a putrid corpse. We have also recognized that his wisdom is worthy of praise in the damnation of the impious, which, drawing good things out of evils, compels those to serve him in punishment who, sinning against justice, were unwilling to be subject in guilt.

Sixth, God’s abundant munificence is worthy of praise in the glorification of the blessed, since for a small merit he rewards his elect with so ineffable a recompense, as though he gave them an immortal gift with the holy angels.

Seventh, the incomprehensible excellence of God is worthy of praise in itself, which orders all things according to his providence and, in [unclear], always without motion or time, remains immovable. The contemplation of this seventh consideration pertains to the sabbath of eternal felicity, in which there is no longer the operation of laborious activity, but the blessedness of a happy, eternal dwelling and rest. Indeed, just as God, creator of all things, is read to have completed all his work on the seventh day and to have rested, so not labor but eternal rest will be imposed upon the just in the heavenly sabbath. Therefore, if we desire happily to come to the heavenly mansions, let us rest in God alone, in whom the rational creature is perfected by resting; perfected through the adherence of love, it rejoices with the Lord in ineffable union and joy. Henceforth, in order to praise God, let pure devotion seek nothing outside God, since almighty God himself, perfect and most wise, suffices for all as the matter of his praise, and exceeds all praise by his infinite perfections. For Scripture says: Praise the Lord as much as you can; he will still surpass. For he is greater than all praise; and therefore he is to be praised by us most humbly in himself and for himself rather than from creatures.

From the aforesaid considerations about God there arises a manifold and varied affection of devotion, through which also a more worthy effect of prayer is generated according to the desire of the affection. For when meditation of the heart is taken up concerning the majesty or power of God, reverent wonder is produced. But when we begin from his unutterable wisdom, confused by our [unclear] imperfection, we accuse ourselves. Thus consequently, from consideration of the mercy of God, hope of pardon is aroused

is obtained: from his patience love of the heart is generated; from justice humility is born; from meditation on munificence, gratitude. For just as, according to the quality of the wood, a kindled fire increases in size, so according to various meditations on God the ardor of devotion rises up in prayers among those who love God.

On meditation upon the aid of our restoration in the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Root II.

The second root of the fear and love of God is generated in meditation on our redemption [unclear], which is produced through diligent exercise in the life, conduct, teaching, and Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. Among all meditations we believe this one to be more useful for us, in which we know our salvation and the sum of eternal happiness to be contained. And [unclear] that the Passion of the Lord, as to its procedure, was unjust; as to its manner, ignominious; as to its pain, bitter; and as to its effect, fruitful, and therefore it must always be kept in memory.

First, as to its procedure, it was unjust, because he who was born of a virgin neither contracted sin nor committed it, nor was deceit found in his mouth. For death is inflicted on us for sin; but he could not justly die, who without any sin was always just and innocent. Indeed, contrary to human law a man is killed if a sentence of death is passed upon one who has neither confessed nor been convicted of a crime. For the Savior was accused before Pilate on three charges: that, calling himself king, he forbade tribute to Caesar; third, that he made himself the Son of God. Of the first two the Gospel speaks, and the accusation is shown to be false. For regarding the first, the contrary was manifestly clear, since Christ said that his kingdom was not earthly. The falsity of the second also did not escape Pilate, who was not ignorant that Jesus had commanded that the things which were Caesar’s be given to Caesar. When asked by the governor about the third, he was silent, because Pilate was unworthy to hear of the divine generation of Jesus, or even of his human birth.

His Passion also stood contrary to custom, because it received no delay of time. He is not placed in prison according to custom; nothing is deliberated in his case; but once captured he is immediately dragged to the judge to be subjected to death; scourged, spat upon, and afflicted with many injuries, blows, and mockeries, he is nailed fast on the cross. Third, it was contrary to the law of nature, and procured from obstinate hatred of heart. For nature forbids raging against the dead, and shudders at lacerating with new blows a body already slain. For after the Redeemer [unclear] had died on the cross, he is pierced with a lance; and contrary to the law of nature, after death he is wounded by the impious.

Second, the Passion of Christ is said to have been ignominious as to its manner, for the six reasons that follow. First, because of the paltry price, since blood of incomparable price is sold by a disciple for thirty pieces of silver, for which no one would deign to sell his little ass. Second, because of the ignominious service, since, full of wounds, he is compelled to carry his cross while half-dead, [unclear]. Thieves and criminal murderers are punished for their own deserts. Fourth, because of the ignominious punishment, since he is hung naked on the cross, a penalty owed only to thieves and criminal men. Indeed, as Scripture says, the Redeemer of the world was condemned by a most shameful death. Fifth, because of the ignominious mockery, since he is hung naked on the cross before the whole multitude and is blasphemed by all as though foolish and insane. Of this the psalmist says: “All day long my shame is before me.” Sixth, because of the ignominious company, since, reckoned with the wicked, he is hung in the midst of thieves. What are you doing now, O Christian soul? Behold, your Savior hangs in the midst among thieves, and you do not fear to sit in the first place in council?

Third, the most holy Passion of Christ, as to its pain, [was] most bitter

[unclear] was: for seven reasons. First, because of the delicate liveliness of his flesh, which in its natural complexion was most excellent, and therefore was more grievously afflicted in the endurance of pains. For delicate flesh suffers more than flesh that is coarse by natural condition. Therefore, since Christ's flesh was subtle and delicate, he poured forth bloody sweat in the garden. Second, because of the character of those who killed him, since Christ was not killed by strangers, but by his own blood-relatives and nearest kin, as earlier he complained through the prophet: "My people, what have I done to you?" For one suffers more tolerably at the hands of strangers and enemies than at the hands of one's own people, since at least friends, by reason of nearness of blood, suffer with one. Third, because of the bitterness of the passion, since he is more afflicted in those places in which pain is felt more strongly because of the nerves. For, raised up on the cross, he is fastened through hands and feet; the Lord of all is given gall and [unclear] to drink. For the psalmist says of him: "They have pierced my hands and my feet; they have counted all my bones." Who could conceive in mind the pain of your most holy heart, good Jesus, when the hardest nails began so cruelly to pierce your hands and feet? Would that my soul might always show itself grateful to you; would that the remembrance of your most holy passion might not depart from my memory. I shall easily be able to obtain from you the effect of my prayers if it should happen that I take delight without interruption in the exercise of your passion. Let each person think what he can; I prefer the memory of your passion to all exercises, through which I trust that in prayers I shall receive whatever is fitting for salvation. Fourth, because of its long duration, the passion of Christ was most bitter, since from the hour of his capture until death he was always in most bitter torment. "All day," he says, "I went about sorrowful, and there is no health in my flesh." Fifth, because of the universality of the passion, since in all the things in which Christ could suffer, he suffered in a singular way. For he suffers in reputation, since, falsely accused, he is blasphemed by the impious. He also suffered in possessions, since he is suspended naked and stripped upon the wood, and his garments are divided by lot among the soldiers. He suffers in soul, since, foreseeing the bitterness of the passion, he was sorrowful even unto death. He suffered in his whole body, since from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there was no health in him. He suffers in his friends, since he is betrayed by a disciple, and, deserted by all, is even publicly denied by Peter. He is afflicted also in compassion with his mother, whose most holy soul, it is remembered, the sword of sorrow pierced. He suffered from the ingratitude of many, since he foresaw that the death which he endured out of compassion for all would be lost in many reprobates. Finally, he suffered in all the senses, as we are taught from the Gospel. He suffers in the eyes, which, with many tears poured forth, are covered with a little cloth. He suffers in hearing, when, amid many insults and outrages, he is mocked and blasphemed. He suffers in smell, since he is defiled with the foul spittle of the Jews. He suffers in touch, since he is tormented in all the members of his body. He suffers in taste, since, being thirsty, he is given gall and vinegar to drink. Sixth, because of the cause of the passion, which was solely the injury done by the Jews, since he suffered wholly without fault. For indeed whoever suffers unjustly is tormented much more in spirit. But the innocent Son of God dies for our sins and is tormented for our crimes, as is read in Isaiah: "Truly he bore our infirmities." Seventh, because of the lack of all consolation, since Christ found no one consoling him in his passion. For he says in the psalm: "You have put far from me friend and neighbor, and my acquaintances because of misery." Indeed, his own stood far off from him.

Fourth, the passion of Christ was fruitful with regard to its effect, which must be considered principally in three things. For first there was the remission of sins; second, the bestowal of grace; third, the presentation of glory. And these three things are indicated by the title affixed to the cross, which, as the evangelist says, contained the cause of the passion of Jesus: "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews." For "Jesus," saving sinners, pertains to the first; "of Nazareth," conferring the flower of grace, to the second; "King of the Jews," presenting the heavenly kingdom to those who confess him, to the third.

Moreover, in this second root we have arranged meditations on the passion of the Lord for each of the hours of the seven days of the week; we have placed them after the end of the third region for this reason: lest in this place we disturb the order of the things to be said by their excessive length. For what we have now set out, we perceive to pertain rather to reading than to meditation, and therefore we postpone those meditations.

On Meditation on the Benefits of God. Root III.

The third root of divine fear and love is fixed in meditation on the benefits of God, through which one comes to the grace of devotion. For the beginning of devotion is placed in meditation on the benefits of God, from the remembrance of which love is generated. The middle, as progress within that meditation itself, desires nothing other than to please God above all things, from whom it knows itself to have been anticipated, without merit, by many benefits. But the end loves God above all things with burning desire and pure fervor of mind, and longs to cling there continually to him alone, without intermediary. And although merciful God has conferred many things specially on each one of us, nevertheless, because we are writing this our [synthema] not for one person but for many, we must set forth not particular benefits assigned to individuals, but general benefits allotted to all, repeatedly and at length. Therefore we comprise the more important ones under the number seven, so that through the seven days of the week, or even in the canonical hours themselves, we may have ready at hand material for meditating daily. But if anyone cannot ascend to that summit of theory, let him strive to exercise himself more fervently in these meditations on the benefits of God, so that, while he diligently continues in the lower things, being purified he may ascend stronger to the higher. Therefore let the cenobite devoutly [remember?] what he has received, so that he may be able to show himself grateful. Let him render to God what he has received, if he longs to be good.

For first he gave us body and soul with their adornments; and those whom he created intellectual, in his own image, he also mercifully called to the heavenly kingdoms. What more could he have given us, who, after creating us when we did not exist, gave himself? But what can we render to our Creator, who by our own merit are sinners and weak? Let us render what we are; let us render what we owe: namely, faithful service for the body that we have received from the Lord, and sincere love for the soul by which we were created in the image of God. For thus the prophet admonishes us in the psalm: Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. Serve faithfully; love reverently. On the part of the body, offer faithful service to your Creator; and on the part of the soul, love him with all your strength. Serve him because the Lord is powerful and great; love him because he is good. His power is shown in your creation; his goodness is declared in your restoration. Since, when you did not exist, he created you by his power, he deserves faithful service; he restored the fallen by his goodness, he deserves the sincere affection of love. For truly he is our Father through love; he is Lord through incomprehensible power.

Second, he gave us faith with the sacraments; for just as he created us without our will, so he called us to the faith without our merit. For Christ says to his disciples in the holy Gospel: You did not choose me, but I chose you. Through faith the Christian soul is led back to its beginning; the sacraments that he gave, we are bound to maintain with perpetual adherence and to remain continually in his holy covenant. For in baptism we renounced the devil and all his pomps; we promised that we would adhere forever to Christ, those who lifted us from the sacred font standing as sureties for us before the Lord in the faith of our parents. Therefore let us always say from the heart with the prophet: It is good for me to adhere to God, to place my hope in the Lord God.

Third, almighty God gave us the art of rectitude and the teachings of truth. For these we owe our Creator faithful execution and perpetual service without fraud.

We are therefore commanded first of all to do everything for the praise of God, and in everything that we do to raise our intention chiefly to his honor. For only a good intention toward God distinguishes works; love alone makes them fruitful. Behold, the Lord has conferred on us the art of nature for praising him; moreover he has given the teachings of salvation through the law; he requires from us praise and love above all things. Let us therefore exercise, for the honor of God, the art conferred on us, and through the teaching of the law the eye of intention will become pure.

Fourth, the merciful Father has conferred on us the world with its necessary elements; for these he requires from us a sincere contemplation of himself as our due. Whatever we see in this world ought to bring us to the remembrance of God, and continually stir us to love its Creator above all things. Hence Bernard, practiced in sacred matters, says: The whole and true lover of God, wherever he turns, has a familiar reminder of his Creator, and uses things as a mirror, and by thinking thus is lifted up from creatures to the Creator. For concerning each thing he says: If those things seem good, beautiful, and sweet which, created with time, are changed and pass away, what goodness, beauty, and sweetness does their author, God, have, remaining forever, who has reserved for himself things incomparably better than these? By this consideration of things the devout person looks upon all human beings with the simple eye of the mind as a likeness of the image of God, and does not curiously attend to the pleasing or displeasing form of the body in them. For in a human being he considers not what he sees outwardly, but the image of the Creator, which he knows to be a sharer in eternal happiness.

Fifth, the Son of God offered himself for us in torments, and redeemed us, lost as we were, from the destruction of perpetual death by his blood. We are commanded to offer a willing imitation to this love of our Savior, if we desire to come to his kingdom. For the prince of the apostles says to the faithful: Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps. What shall I repay to you, O good Jesus, for your benefits toward me, so great and so immeasurable? I shall suffer with you in heart, I shall suffer with you in deed; I shall imitate you in the affections of the mind according to my ability.

Sixth, the Creator has conferred on us the time for meriting eternal life; he [gave?] the necessary nourishment of the body. For here we are debtors to ourselves, since in this time we owe ourselves the acquisition [of merit?]. Why then do we spend the days of salvation so negligently and without the fruit of merit, when we have nothing more precious than time? Behold, within a brief time now we can merit the joys of eternal happiness, and all of us neglect to do what is good. Woe to us, foolish and insane, who have received nothing in this world more precious than time, and yet are accustomed to spend nothing more cheaply. For now an acceptable time is granted to us; now the day of salvation is bestowed, in which we ought to devote ourselves to holy works with the greatest fervor, and always to [provide for?] the hour of death.

Seventh, he set before us all heaven, filled with joys, and promised himself, together with the things contained in it, as rewards. For this munificence of our Savior we ought to devote ourselves to the holy works of mercy and, according to our strength, show ourselves imitators of God. To this he exhorts us in his sacred Gospels: Be merciful, as your Father God also is merciful. At the end also, when the day of judgment has come, the merciful, as the Lord himself promises, will go into eternal life, since whoever has done mercy will obtain mercy. And lest someone from among the monks say to me, “I can show mercy to no one, since the religious life permits me to possess absolutely nothing,” let us know that among the necessary works of mercy the spiritual are the more powerful. If you, monk, wish to be merciful, pray to God for the wretched; bestow saving teaching upon the unlearned.

Therefore the sum of meditation on the benefits of God rests upon three exercises, in which it is principally contained whole. In the first, indeed, we ought to attribute all things to God, not to ourselves; in the second, by remembering the benefits of God, to exercise ourselves in the pursuit of love; in the third, [unclear] concerning the benefits received

[Preceding page illegible in the source.]

…[it] cannot [become better]: because neither does the best become better, nor the greatest become greater. God created you by his goodness, not because your creation was necessary to him, but advantageous to you alone. He who considers this goodness of God with intent meditation deservedly praises his Creator.

Secondly, lest you be lifted up into pride, O man, consider the vileness of your condition: that you were made from the slime of the earth, and after a little while, consumed by worms, you will return into dust in the earth. Why then are you proud, [you] earth and ashes? Your conception has fault; [your] nativity, misery; [your] life, penalty; the dissolution of death, anguish. For man, born of woman, living a short time, is filled with many miseries; and then he is most miserable, when he does not acknowledge himself miserable in the flesh.

Thirdly, consider the origin of your conception, and you will find your soul stained with the foul turpitude of original sin. For we are born children of wrath; but, obtaining the grace of baptism in the blood of Christ Jesus, we are cleansed from the original stain. Deservedly do we love our Savior through this consideration, by whose mercy we have been cleansed from the original stain.

Fourthly, consider, O faithful soul, how exceedingly vile you have been made, repeating your ways in the act of sin: since you have shown yourself an adulteress to Christ your spouse, when he had joined you to himself—wholly immaculate—by his blood. What do you do, O wretched one? Why do you desert your most loving spouse, or why, foolish, do you withdraw from your beginning? Know that you are placed in the flesh—not that you should consent to its vices and concupiscences, but rather that you should resist [them] by the command of reason. For as often as you shall have surrendered your consent (so to speak, by dissembling) to the inordinate motions of the flesh, contrary to divine rectitude, so often, turned away from the supreme good and from your spouse, you show yourself an adulteress. Beware, beware, O soul redeemed by the blood of Christ, lest the love of the flesh deceive you; for, just as the first man, deceived by love of his consort woman, fell into death, so any soul whatever, consenting to the pleasures of its flesh, basely withdraws from its beginning, which is God. But, alas, wretched [soul], how have you fallen? You have dwelt in a foreign land; you have been defiled with the dead; you have been counted with those descending into hell. You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom; you have been turned backward; adulter[y]…

you have committed. But hear my counsel, and return as quickly as possible to Jesus, the guide of your youth; submit yourself wholly and humbly to him. He is merciful: he will gladly receive you as you return to him; he will forgive your vices, and, if you ask, will bestow the grace of his love. But you must withdraw from the affections of the flesh, if you desire to come into the sight of your Savior. Therefore, if you turn to Jesus, turn in truth, because supreme Truth cannot love anything except what is true.

There is also another mode of self-knowledge, which is taken up with respect to God, whenever the incomparable comparison between God and man is contemplated. Concerning this mode Bernard, illustrious in contemplation, says: Never does the measure of human imperfection better detect itself than in the light of God’s countenance and the mirror of divine vision. For there, he who is more in the day, and sees more what is lacking in himself, day by day amends by likeness whatever he has done wrong by unlikeness, drawing near through likeness to him from whom he was made far off through unlikeness. Therefore let us raise the gaze of the mind to the super-bright mirror of divine perfection; let us submit our affection to that unchangeable good, so that in God’s wisdom we may be able to detect our own foolishness, and in his power consider our own weakness.

On Keeping the Memory of One’s Sins. Root V.

The fifth root of the fear of God is the memory of sins, and the very foulness of sin often pondered. For indeed, he who truly understands the shamefulness of mortal sin always greatly fears the pit of this evil. But so that you may in some way recognize the gravity of sin, you must consider the seven things that follow.

First, then, consider the beauty of God’s justice, to which sin is wholly contrary, and therefore to be fled above all. For through sin the soul is entirely turned away from the highest good, and the love that is naturally in it toward its own beginning is changed into hatred.

For just as all good things are from the first good, so every love, toward whatever good it may be directed, is naturally kindled by the same good. For since our love cannot rest in any goods as in its end, it has as its end, where it is to rest, the same good that it had also as its beginning. Therefore, whenever sin is committed against the beauty of God’s justice, the mind is separated from its own beginning. For since God is charity, he demands love in the soul; peace requires peace; like loves like; unlike hates unlike.

Second, consider the enormity of sin, and carefully weigh how much its foulness displeases God. Behold, because of pride, the just God cast the most noble angel Lucifer out of heaven, and condemned him with his accomplices to the burning of eternal fire. He also compelled our first parents, Adam and Eve, to leave paradise because of disobedience, and by just judgment condemned the whole human race, in their crime, to the sentence of a twofold death. Finally, let us turn over the whole history of the Old and New Testament, and we shall find that what was clearly committed rashly against God’s justice was often gravely punished by that justice. Therefore the gravity of the crime is easily recognized, if the severity of the vengeance that followed is considered.

Third, consider how grave a scandal arises from sin, especially when one sins before others. For he who by his own evil example provokes someone to sin shows himself to be an adversary of God. For God, by his own will and out of mercy, disposed to save souls redeemed by the blood of his Only-Begotten; this man, through evil example and out of aversion from God, desires to destroy them. But the sin of scandal, with respect to guilt, is for this reason called very grave: because, as we have said, it is opposed to God. But if the one who gives occasion for harm is to be thought to have caused the harm, the sinner subjects himself to be condemned by as many sentences of death as he has made men fall into mortal crime by his own evil example. For Christ says in the holy Gospel: Woe to the man through whom scandal comes. And again he says: He who shall scandalize one of these little ones in

for those who believe in me: it is expedient for him that a millstone be hung about his neck, and that he be sunk in the depth of the sea. Rare is the true repentance of one who scandalizes the little ones, because, when he neglects to make restitution for the harm done to another, he by no means attains to the fruit of saving repentance.

Fourth, consider the negligence of your ungrateful heart, since you, who were created in the image of God and ought to have loved your maker above all things, dishonor him in many ways by your sins. To Christ the Son of God, by whose blood you have been redeemed, you ought to render continual service of love; but you do not fear to love the flesh more than Jesus Christ your savior. Finally, with a compassionate mind you ought daily to turn over in your mind his most holy passion, and yet you are accustomed to think of nothing less than of it. Adopted among the sons of God by mercy alone, you ought to have shown yourself worthy of the heavenly calling as an imitator, and still you do not fear to lie through sloth in the lowest things. And why do I say much? Behold, you who have been marked with the Holy Spirit, who have been counted with the angels, are called to the inheritance of the sons of God; you are invited by all the saints to the feasts of paradise; you partake daily of the body and blood of our savior Jesus Christ; and yet you do not observe the commandments of God and of the rule which you promised, so that you might be blessed. Examine your conscience carefully, therefore, and you will find that there are many good things you ought to do and omit, and many evil things you ought to omit and commit against God's good pleasure.

Fifth, consider whom you offend by sinning: not a man, but God; not a creature, but the Creator. He against whom you have sinned is great and immeasurable, terrible and glorious; his majesty the angels tremble at, his power all the heavenly spirits marvel at. To the highest and unchangeable good, God, the beginning and end of every creature, the rational spirit ought to devote love and the desire of adhesion beyond human understanding, and to raise itself wholly to that truly one thing, as to its own center, despising all phantasms; and it can lift itself up to this so much the more easily, the more, leaving all other things behind, it has striven to unite itself to itself alone. For by the power of that one itself, wherever union occurs, nor for any other reason are things more alike more easily united to one another than because they are one in quality. Therefore the soul is then at last most rightly said to be united with the one principle of things when it, having been made [most purely?] one in itself, is separated from every multitude and, above all imagination, reason, and understanding, its unity alone escapes, enjoying through loving affection the unity of God, joining, so to speak, its own center with the center of the universe. But when the human soul itself, suffering badly along with its flesh as if with its spouse, is turned toward any animal passions, then that very unity is badly changed into a multitude contrary to the one alone, and it becomes so much the more remote from its principle as it has been divided from itself. Finally, the soul itself contracts a great difficulty in returning to that one ineffable divine thing whenever, confused in itself, it falls into the sin of apostasy. Think now how great and ineffable he is against whose honor sin is committed; and since you are wholly unable to understand the greatness of his majesty, learn humbly to fear his power.

Sixth, consider what you have lost by sinning, so that the recognized greatness of the loss may hasten repentance and restore through tears what has been lost. What, then, wretched man, have you lost by sinning? Hear what you have lost. You had been made like God through grace, the companion of angels, a member of Christ, and chosen heir of eternal happiness; you ought to have lived and rejoiced without end in the goods of the Lord with all the saints. But what has happened with your sin? You have been compared to senseless beasts, and have been made like them. For when you were in honor, you were unwilling to understand; you abandoned the fountain of life; by sinning you have been made the companion and member of the devil, the harlot of Antichrist, the heir of hell. You abandoned life; you chose everlasting death. If you fear the sentence, change your will, and you will find remission.

Seventh, consider what you have deserved by sinning, since if eternal death is inflicted for one sin, he who has many, not to say in-

has committed innumerable things, consider what he deserves. For the soul that has sinned, it itself shall die. Moreover, even by one mortal sin you have deserved to be the devil’s companion without end, to be deprived of all the joys of heaven, to be burned forever in the fires of hell. These are the rewards which sin has brought you; these the gifts which it promised.

Now therefore from these seven considerations make a plaster for the wounded soul; take up for yourself the goad of compunction, so that you may come to the root of fear. But hasten, and do not put it off from day to day, since he who receives the humble confession of the penitent has not promised tomorrow to the one who delays. For where haste finds pardon, delay often cuts off life. Hope of a longer life draws many to destruction, because, while they trust that they can live longer in this world, they make the time of penitence pass without penitence. But you, man, if you accept my counsel, do not defer penitence, since you do not know what tomorrow may bring you. For he deserves to lose the time of penitence who so often does not fear to defer his pursuit.

On present vanity and eternity, the sixth root.

The sixth root of fear is raised up in the mind of the one meditating, if the vanity of visible things and the eternity of invisible things are considered with zealous intention. For all things which we behold in this world are wholly subject to vanity and corruption, and indeed will last for a very short time. All mortal things hang upon uncertain chance, and by their own changeableness promise flight. Whatever you have today will perhaps leave you tomorrow; or even now, while you are speaking, it will cease to be yours. For we perceive nothing in this world long-lasting and stable, but see all things change with time.

Ascend now, therefore, the watchtower of your mind, O faithful monk, and consider how all things which time contains are nothing, since whatever visible thing is now perceived will soon be corrupted. Take from things past a consideration of things present, and see that what has passed away is not, and what now seems to be will not be after a little while. Where are the kings of the nations, where the princes, where the leaders, where the rich, where those once powerful in the world? Where are all the lovers of the world; where are the men who despised the arduous way of heaven? Finally, where are all those once known to you in the world, whom death meanwhile snatched away while you were in the cloister? Behold, from the origin of the world, both those who lived for many times and those who lived for few, all died in their own generation; and according to the diversity of their merits, with justice dictating, they also received diverse rewards. The lovers of God receive everlasting bright dwellings, filled with inestimable joys, associated with the creator of all; and the worshippers of the world, despising God’s commandments, once swollen here with honors, puffed up with knowledge, immersed in riches, given over to pleasures and vices, have descended to hell to be tormented without end. What harm, I ask, does that once laborious contempt of the world, contrary to the flesh, now do to the saints in heaven, for which they already enjoy forever the glad vision of God? Or what profit now to the impious buried in hell is the consolation of the flesh once possessed, for which they now receive the torments of eternal damnation? Think on these things while it is profitable; meditate on these things while the opportunity of taking care is present.

Again, ascending higher, try with the gaze of the mind, as far as you can, to fix your eyes on the abyss of infinite depth, and to consider how long that is which is eternal. Eternal is a time which is enclosed by no end, bounded by no space. The saints of God, blessed, will exult forever in glory; sinners, wretched, will burn forever in hell. O eternal name, terrible without end, who will be able to think on you or speak you without fear? Truly, whoever thinks on you never sins forever. The eternal has no end. Hear a comparison, and, since it will not be sufficient for eternity, receive fear. If a heap of sand were placed in the size of Mount Olympus, stretching all the way to heaven, from which after ten thousand years only one grain were [unclear] by a small

a little bird would [wear it away?]; that mountain would by no means be said to be going to last forever, but would be subject to an end, and, although after innumerable years, nevertheless destined someday to cease. Yet all that time during which something of the mountain remained, however very long it was, would nevertheless seem, relatively, to be nothing in comparison with eternity. For eternity admits neither the imagining of an end, nor the hope of completion, nor a limit.

O therefore how foolish, how senseless, how mad is the man who casts aside this consideration of eternity, and spends uselessly the acceptable time granted to him for meriting eternal goods. The hour will come, and already hastens near, in which the wretched man will learn what eternity is, when he will no longer be able to do better. But you, my monk, who desire to be faithful, cast away from yourself all anxiety for the world. Set all your care toward the love of God. Do nothing, think nothing, except what can lead you to the love of your Creator, or what you know pertains to the edification of others or to the pure necessity of the body. Separate yourself, I pray, from the lowest things, so that, being good, you may be delighted by eternal things. Let no anxiety of the flesh remove you from the inward tranquillity of mind; let no pleasure corrupt you. Strive always, as much as you are able, to persist in prayers with devotion, and again, through the affection of love, to raise yourself more frequently.

On Always Having Zeal for God.

The Seventh Root of Fear. Root VII. The monk is commanded to exercise himself in this no little.

For no one who truly loves his lord tolerates with equanimity injuries done to him. You therefore, monk, who desire to be a faithful servant of Jesus Christ, do not neglect zeal for him within yourself. When you see an injury to God, do not conceal it, because whoever does not at once resist those who disparage him is proved to love his lord less. Let men know you as such a lover of God and enemy of vices that they do not dare to speak evil before you, nor presume to do anything evil while you look on.

Be conspicuous in uprightness of soul, renowned for the merit of your life, venerable in zeal. Let the righteous love you as a servant of God; let the reprobate dread your face as a judge. Let no one presume to do anything in your sight that is alien to good morals, since indeed all know that you cannot tolerate an injury to God. Thus Phinehas merited the everlasting priesthood, when by zeal for the law he powerfully appeased the wrath of the Lord. If you see order perishing in the monastery, and if your brothers have begun in any way to corrupt regular observance, do not, if you are a servant of God, keep silence about their vices. Set yourself firmly against them, with strength, for the house of the Lord. Exercise zeal for God as much as you can; destroy the counsels of the malicious; resist the rashness of the proud. If you are a true lover of God, by your face alone you will scatter the gatherings of the depraved. For no one will lay bare his counsel before you if he suspects your zeal to be opposed to him. But if the evil and reprobate, while doing evil, do not fear your presence, assuredly they recognize no zeal for God in you. Therefore, that you may show yourself a true servant of Christ, you ought willingly, for love of God, to forgive your brothers the injuries inflicted on you, and to beseech God for those very persons who injure you. But it is not yours to forgive injuries done to your Lord without his will, but rather to avenge them out of zeal for uprightness. In these matters let love of blood cease; let the bond of friendship give way far off. Zeal for God is rightly to be preferred to all things. For friendship with man is to be observed in such a way that it is never preferred to zeal for God.

Woe to monks and abbots who so boldly cast aside zeal for God; who put familiarities with men before the divine command; who conceal the vices of their subjects through foolish compassion; who observe the traditions of the holy rule neither in themselves nor in others. And what shall I say? We see among cloistered monks that obedience to commands is despised, zeal for uprightness scorned, observance of the rule contemned. Two or more enter among themselves into a covenant of carnal friendship under the name of charity; the infirm entrust their diseases of soul to those more infirm, and

they by no means seek the friendship of God through purity of mind. Each one thinks his own companion better than the rest; and each, deceived, loves the other not spiritually but carnally, since they do not raise their affections to God: they love nothing but the consolations of the flesh. But the monk whom you see seeking the friendship of weak brethren you must regard not as a servant of God but as a lover of the flesh. For he who truly occupies his whole heart in the love of God cares nothing for human friendship. The love of Jesus suffices him for all things; apart from him he seeks nothing further. But he who has sought consolation of mind in outward things shows by his deed that he does not love God with his whole heart. The love of God loves solitude, hates the tumults of men, and does not seek the conversations of friends. O good Jesus, how sweet is your love, since it penetrates the heart of him who loves you; seeing you, the soul longs [to see] you; possessing you, it desires to embrace you. For truly he who loves you forgets his very self; he meditates on nothing but the sweetest presence of you. There is nothing in the world that pleases one who loves you; nowhere is there found anything that the soul desires besides you. O with how many sighs the mind wounded by love is distressed; with what most abundant tears the face is watered in secret, because as often as it thinks of the face of the beloved presiding in heaven, so often it laments itself desolate on earth. Meanwhile the languishing mind often tries to say something of its most beloved Jesus; it strives also to provoke others to love of him; but as soon as it has begun to utter the sweetest name of Jesus, unwillingly, because of the greatness of love, it falls silent. For the love of Jesus is expressed by no words, but is felt with sweetness in the secrecy of the mind. I know one who said: My love has been crucified. Who is your love, O servant of God? Why do you weep? Why do you groan? Ignatius: My love has been crucified, and shall I not mourn? My Lord has died, and shall I be able to restrain my tears? Do not weep, O faithful soul; for although your love died in order to redeem you from death, yet now he has risen from the dead, that in heaven [he may give] the crown of life. Be faithful unto death, and he will give you the crown of life.

On the manner and degrees of divine love, comprising the conclusion of this second region.

Since no one suddenly becomes the highest, nor can anyone by his own powers suddenly ascend to that supreme summit of divine love, I now think it useful briefly to note the fixed manners or degrees themselves of loving God.

Therefore, for moving the human heart to divine love, the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, in my judgment, is more effective than all other things, if it has been meditated upon in a man’s mind purely, sweetly, fervently, perseveringly, and diligently. For truly, he who often recalls to memory, with compassion and thanksgiving, the life, Passion, and death of our Savior according to the chief principal articles, prepares a swift ascent of the heart to divine love. But this most holy occupation of the mind concerning the Passion of the Lord we shall treat opportunely in the second principal part of the work, where we shall set forth more broadly the manner of spiritual exercise. But so far as the account of what has been said pertains in this place, I find three manners of loving God, which I shall briefly explain in order.

The first manner commands that you love him who loves you, that you join your whole self to him sweetly, so that your heart loves nothing outside God and seeks nothing from elsewhere. For since God is wholly simple, he alone desires to possess the whole heart of the lover; he drives it far from dissipated thoughts. Therefore if you wish to love sweetly, love wholly. For the love of God makes either everything perfect or nothing. Let meditation on the Passion of Jesus Christ our Savior possess you wholly, until love sweetly grows strong in you. You must despise everything in the flesh that flatters, if you desire to arrive at the love of God. For no one can sweetly love God in this life so long as he strives to love anything in the world. Indeed, love of the world is utterly contrary to divine love, since where one is admitted to the inner chambers of the heart, the other is forbidden to be present. But how great a sweetness, how great a delight, and how great a joy of mind the love of God in

No one at all understands what it begets in the heart of the lover, except the one who, having despised all the things and events of the world, has loved God alone for a long time. The heart of one who loves God loves none of the things that are in the world; it despises the riches, honors, and favor of the age; it is not afraid to undergo any adversities for the love of its Lord. The love of God is never idle; it always desires to come to its source; it refuses to endure no labors in this world. Therefore let him love who does not wish to become slothful. One's neighbor too is to be loved sweetly on account of God, and by no reasoning is he to be offended against God or justice. Let each person always show himself to his brother, in words and deeds, such as he expects others to be toward himself. For he truly loves his neighbor who, for his sake, exposes his goods, body, and soul. This Christ taught; this the Son of God did for us. Indeed, he who says that he truly believes in Christ ought himself also to walk just as He walked. He does not truly love Christ who does not keep His commandments. For He says: This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you. We are members of one head, Jesus Christ; we then believe in Him when we observe His commandment concerning love toward God and toward our neighbor. Let us therefore love our neighbor, because he is a member in Christ together with us, so that just as one member in the body suffers with another, so a brother may be humbly helped by a brother for the love of Christ. The second mode commands you to love wisely, and to seek nothing else in divine love but God. Extend your affection toward that Word which was in the beginning with God; lift your mind above everything that is created, because unless you leave behind yourself and all things that are in the world, you will not be able to come to Him whom you love. Finally, if you desire to love God wisely, do not think yourself, O man, to be anything, because where a man thinks himself to be something, he already loves unwisely. The third mode commands that you love strongly, and never be afraid to expose body and soul for the love of God.

He is not a strong lover of God who is afraid to undergo death for Him. For love is strong as death. One's neighbor is loved wisely if not the man but the vice is hated. But he is loved strongly if every injury is forgiven from a heart intending to do good to him.

The second region ends.

Preface to the third treatise of the first part, which describes the highest region of the spirit of cloistered persons.

At last, as I am about to write, with the Lord’s help, of that highest region of the spirit, I am shaken by fear and shame alike, because, being small, I fear to speak of the greatest things, and I am much ashamed to teach what I have not sufficiently experienced. For what intellect, however practiced, of any man could apprehend the state of a mind sweetly resting in God through love? Or what speech, even of the most eloquent orator, could explain the secret sweetness of inward contemplation? Indeed, the exercise of this third region surpasses human understanding for the greater part; in it the mind of a purified man, through the fervor of divine love, is caught up above itself, and, while its natural essence remains, is absorbed, lulled by wondrous sweetness, in the abyss of divine contemplation. For it is overwhelmed by such sweetness of inward majesty that it seems unable either to understand or to express its own state. For, having abandoned sensory operation, it wholly passes beyond even the intellectual; and, what is more, abandoning itself, without imagination, reason, or understanding, it is lifted by affection above itself to that highest summit of the divine darkness.

But when it has utterly failed away from itself, it does not act but rests; nor, when returned to itself, can it understand what it has undergone, nor reveal to anyone the manner of its elevation. For this elevation of the mind into God is so profound and so sublime that not only can one who has not experienced it not understand it, but not even one who has experienced it can fully explain it in words as it is. But what shall I be able to say about the mountain of divine darkness, which I have not yet deserved to penetrate? For the well of inward contemplation is deep, and I am weak, since I have brought neither a vessel suited to these waters, nor prepared steps [of ascent?] suited to steep places. Well-arranged words do not befit a fool; nor should an unskilled and cold man speak of the secrets of divine contemplation, one who still stands with the weak in the valleys. For only he speaks fruitfully of deep things who is illumined by the double ray of the spirit. Yet since I am a man placed under obedience to the annual chapter, I am compelled to take up the mandate of that synod and to finish, according to my strength, the work set before me. Therefore I enter upon the third region of cloistered persons under the guidance of the venerable father, lord John of Bursfelde, the devout abbot, so that, by bringing back as far as possible to my own manner of speaking what he described in scholastic and truthful discourse, I may seem to have obeyed the chapter.

Here begins the third region of the soul, which is called spiritual, in which the highest tranquillity of mind is possessed.

The third, or highest, region of the soul is called spiritual; in it the highest rest and tranquillity of mind is found. And this region is compared to the empyrean heaven, in which there is the true rest of all and the true blessedness of souls. The spirit established in this region leaves the rational beneath itself, and, lifted up through love, wondrously ascends into God. For whatever is done in this most holy region is judged wholly divine. Here the human spirit, caught up above itself, receives the divine inflowing; and, lulled in the darkness of divine contemplation, withdrawn from all creatures, it sweetly comes to rest. In this region almighty God directs the spirit of the contemplative to himself, and perfects the simplified intellectual powers of the soul, recalled from every phantasm into the inner chamber, according to their tendencies and objects; and, leading the mind stripped of all multiplicity to himself, the one principle, he also makes it one in himself, not by nature but by gracious participation. The citizens of this highest region are truly spiritual men, who, despising all the things and affections of the world, love nothing in this world except God, desire nothing inordinately, but, absorbed by inward affection from

by the divine Spirit, they thirst vehemently for God himself; they burn with ineffable desire for love of him. For they are carried toward God with such fervor of love that, lifted above their very selves, they very often abandon all intellectual operations and, borne into the abyss of divine contemplation, admit absolutely nothing except God; and, existing there insensibly through the grace of love, they become one with God by the gift of participation, while the property of the natures remains preserved. For the holy apostle of Jesus Christ says: “He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit.” And again he says: “Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God.” The same apostle also shows himself to be a citizen of this most holy region, when he cries to the Philippians: “Our conversation is in heaven.” For as long as we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord; but, as if through a dream, we are sweetly led to our homeland when we dwell in heavenly things by mind and spirit. I would say “through a dream” not properly, but by a remote comparison. For in dreams we go forth by images of things intelligible to us, the forms being preserved in the imagination; in contemplation, beyond every imagination, we are raised pure to God in mind and spirit. And therefore this supreme region of the soul is called spiritual; from it all religious obtain the name of spirituality. Woe to us. From this most blessed region we are called spiritual; we are named religious lovers of God, we who nevertheless desire to attain the summit of this mountain through contemplation. In this region charity holds empire, wisdom the consulship; in it nothing is loved except God, nothing is done inordinately. This most holy region belongs to the empyrean heaven, because those whom it spiritually receives as citizens it will send on to the joys of heaven without intermediary. For just as the lowest region of the flesh will send its citizens, when they die, to hell, and the middle region of reason to purgatory, so this one will send its perfect worshippers, when they depart, to heaven. The dignity of this third and supreme region is expressed by many prerogatives and is especially commended in seven articles, as will be said in order.

That This Supreme Region Is the Cloistral Spirit. Article 1.

And first, indeed, this third region of the soul is described by a pleasing comparison, because it is compared to the highest empyrean heaven. For just as all things are tranquil in the empyrean heaven, so on this summit of the supreme region the mind of a man [contemplating?] God is agitated by no disturbances. Here is the highest rest of the contemplating soul; here no crowd of vices dwells; no bitterness of mind comes near. In the empyrean heaven, indeed, the majesty of God is beheld by the holy spirits by an ineffable gift; here, in darkness, through the desire of love, it is seen above understanding. There God is all in all; here nothing among all things pleases except God. There it is granted to the saints to rest from their labors without end; here the mind is permitted, by resting, to foretaste the unspeakable sweetness of inward delight. There is no felicity greater than that in heaven, and there is no tranquillity in the world so sweet as that in this region. Blessed indeed are those who have deserved to ascend this mountain of divine contemplation: they love absolutely nothing in this world; they desire nothing other than always to cleave to God. O how secure is the conscience of such people, how joyful their manner of life, where no evil is committed, where nothing other than that supreme, immutable good is desired. For the mind purified by divine love, which has truly and [fully?] ascended this region, desires nothing carnal, nothing inordinate; it raises itself wholly into contemplation of the highest majesty through desire; it rests sweetly in God alone. O who [unclear] the inward sweetness.

... of one loving [God] could truly express, when the mind recalls the powers and faculties of the soul from the dispersion of multiplicity into one, and raises them upward with burning affections into the chamber of the spirit. Here it directs its gaze and its love toward that immutable good of lights; it utterly rejects from itself every created and creatable multiplicity; the soul gathers itself into one, so that, being one in itself, it may be able to rise without the impediment of multiplicity to the principle of light, which is one. Only unity can clearly attain to the one principle of things, because unity flees multiplicity; the one requires unity. For the more you have yielded to multiplicity, the more you withdraw from unity. Therefore God, for those dwelling in this highest region of the spirit, so that love may be able to rise in contemplation of its principle, is accustomed to renounce from himself every multiplicity clinging in imagination or understanding, so that, gathered in its own unity, it may be able to strive ardently toward that simple [unclear] with the affection of love, which it knows to be above every position.

That this highest region of the spirit is thus sweet and lovable by reason of nearness. Article [unclear].

Second, moreover, this highest region of the spirit is sweet and most pleasant by likeness, indeed with a singular spirit. For the citizen of this most holy region, [unclear] parts, as I might say, separates light as life from the citizens above, because the spirit, while it inhabits the flesh, cries to heaven as though through a wall. But light [unclear] the parts of the flesh [unclear], from which the free spirit, about to migrate to heaven, goes forth when the spirit is separated from the body. But the spirit wounded by sins, which cannot raise itself to this region by a pure affection of love, is still said to stand farther away from the empyrean heaven. Those, however, who dwell in that most quiet region are nearest to the empyrean heaven, because, weighed down by no stains of sins, they despise all earthly and carnal things and always desire to dwell in heavenly things in mind and spirit.

Indeed those who inhabit the empyrean heaven and those who dwell in this third region have one and the same delight. But there is this difference, that for both there is sweetness in contemplating God: here it is great, there it is greatest; here in the desire of fervent love, there in the possession of most blessed vision.

In this highest region of divine contemplation the rational spirit recalls its powers and faculties into its chamber, in which it too, free from every phantasm, is at rest; it raises itself above itself into the dense darkness of the divine, in which, put to sleep by ecstatic love, it rests sweetly. No troublesome confusion of thoughts is stirred here, no imagining of phantasms; rather the naked mind is raised upward and contemplates without any thought or imagination. For truly, when the mind itself opens an entrance to thoughts, it again shows that it is descending to the middle region, which belongs to reason.

But since the human mind cannot always remain unmoved on the summit of divine contemplation, it is necessary that it often return to the rational exercise of the second region. If, however, it has slipped down into sensual passions, then again it descends to the lowest region. But the soul of the true lover of God, although on account of the frailty of the flesh it cannot always remain in the pleasantness of contemplation, nevertheless strives more often, through burning affection, to lift itself to that region, so that it may fulfill the exercise of reason in such a way that it does not wholly omit the sweetness of inward delight. O how good it is to cling to the Lord; how sweet it is to attend to God alone, so that the mind may thirst for the Lord Jesus before all things and always long to embrace him with burning desires. Indeed, one who stands in this region is nearest to the empyrean heaven, and therefore is inflamed toward it with the greatest desires of love.

O how many groans and tears the mind fervent with love is accustomed to send forth; how ardently it sighs for heavenly things; since the nearer it is known to be to the empyrean heaven while standing in this highest region through the secret of contemplation, the more ardent is its affection for leaving the prison of the body. Whence

and, with the holy apostle, the mind, languid with love, says in its fiery sighs: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.”

That this region of the soul is by divine instruction. Article IV.

Third, this supreme region of the soul is said to be by divine instruction: in it the mind, glowing with divine love, is taught not by man but by the Holy Spirit.
